articles.title: Tribal Narratives on Screen: A Study of Stereotypical Semiotics in Tamil Films Viduthalai Part 1 & 2
articles.authors: Divakar P; Abdullah Alfazeena
articles.abstract:
This paper considers the way in which modern Tamil cinema portrays tribal communities, with reference to
Viduthalai Part 1 and Part 2. It pays attention to the signs and symbols which filmmakers make to get a perception
of tribal identity, oppression, and marginalization. Indian cinema seldom allows tribal communities a fair and correct
representation, and this is an issue that has been raised by critics over the years. This study excavates the particular
signs and symbols that these films operate with to narrate the lives, struggles, and identities of the indigenous people.
Historically, tribal groups in India have been driven to the periphery, where they experience a social and economic
pressure. That reality is common in movies, but there are occasions when, rather than the reflective power of a
culture and its capabilities, movies merely reiterate the wide-worn-out clichés of tribes as pathetic victims or exotic
outsiders. Viduthalai is one that is working that line; the movie foreshadows oppression and resistance by the tribes,
but it also demonstrates that it is not an easy task to depict disenfranchised individuals in a cinematic world
realistically. The unique thing is that it is a tendency: such movies tend to reveal the tale of tribal suffering and
resistance in the form of victimization and sacrifice without any stories of strength and endurance. With the help of
the works of film studies and studies about the problems of cultural representation, this paper locates these
presentations within the overall context of how the Indian society and film industry tend to treat the tribal populations.
Semiotics assists in decomposing all this. Using the analysis of the pictures, symbols, and the types of characters
used in these movies, it can be said what indeed is getting through. Viduthalai relies on stereotypes of old, with its
main focus placed on oppression and the lack of more empowering points of view. Such a narrative confines tribal
identities to a very small trap and casts genuine questions with regard to authenticity and morality. The article brings
the discussion to the next level, denouncing the risks of these stereotypes and asking filmmakers to make much more
individual and deep films on tribal life in India. Such signs and signals are not only essential to study, but also, it is
about cultural awareness, social justice, and responsible storytelling. This study urges an improving way: telling
stories that not only repeat tired clichés but also actually glorify the variety and richness of tribal cultures. Film is a
need that affects people within the way of thinking, policy formulation, and even brings a change in the real treatment
of a tribe to the rest of the world. Ultimately, this study is not only a critique but also a form of call to reconsider the
way in which cinema can be culturally ethical and truthful in terms of its qualities to depict any identity.

articles_hidden.title: Book of Abstracts- Media Metamorphosis & AI: Unveiling the Future of Content
articles_hidden.authors: Abdullah Alfazeena; Manikkam K; Jone Antony Raja. J
articles_hidden.abstract: The Book of Abstracts for the International Conference 2025 on “Media Metamorphosis & AI: Unveiling the Future of Content”, organized by the Department of Visual Communication, Hindusthan College of Arts & Science, Coimbatore, is a compilation of scholarly contributions presented during the conference held on 30th October, 2025. This volume showcases a diverse collection of research abstracts from academicians, scholars, and professionals exploring the dynamic relationship between media, artificial intelligence, and digital transformation. The works featured in this book highlight the changing contours of media practices, ethical challenges, creative innovations, and the transformative potential of AI in shaping the future of communication and content creation. It encapsulates multidisciplinary perspectives on how technology continues to redefine the media ecosystem. It serves as a valuable resource for researchers, educators, and practitioners seeking to understand and contribute to the evolving media landscape.

articles_hidden.title: An item bank of reporting items and concepts in evidence synthesis reporting guidelines
articles_hidden.authors: Kyle Morrison; Edward R. Ivimey-Cook; Malgorzata Lagisz; Ayumi Mizuno; Manuela Santos Santana; Eduardo S. A. Santos; Alfredo Sánchez-Tójar; Zachary P. Simpson; Matthew James Grainger; Biljana Macura
articles_hidden.abstract: Evidence synthesis integrates findings from multiple research studies, and its value for decision making depends on complete, transparent reporting. Authors often rely on reporting guidelines, checklists, flow diagrams, or structured text guiding manuscript reporting, but they still struggle to implement what counts as clear, complete reporting. A central issue is that many guidelines address the same underlying concepts using different wording, making it unclear whether differences between guidelines are meaningful or merely semantic. To address this, we compiled an item bank of 2,249 reporting items from 59 unique evidence synthesis reporting guidelines (from 83 studies, 68 checklists), using a six-step process: literature searching and screening, item collation, readability analysis, concept extraction, and overlap assessment. Compiled items were relatively verbose (mean words/item = 19.9) and linguistically complex (Moving-Average Type-Token Ratio = 0.959), indicating limited reuse of consistent wording—likely making items harder to interpret and compare. Because items can contain multiple concepts, and concepts can recur across items and guidelines, we identified 403 unique reporting concepts. Guidelines also showed modest conceptual overlap (Jaccard Similarity Index = 0.166, n = 1,830 pairwise comparisons), suggesting some concepts were widely shared across reporting guidelines for different methodologies and disciplines, pointing to clear potential to harmonise reporting guidance and reduce duplicated effort. We provide all reporting items and concepts in the supplementary files. We further discuss trends and gaps in item use and wording across guidelines, outline applications of the collated item bank, and note limitations that point to future research. Together, our findings offer much-needed direction for developing and harmonising future reporting guidelines, an essential step toward more consistent and transparent reporting across evidence synthesis.

articles_hidden.title: The NF Data Portal: A Community-Driven Resource to Accelerate Neurofibromatosis and Schwannomatosis Research and Drug Development
articles_hidden.authors: Kara Quaid; Belinda B. Garana; Chang In Moon; Aditya Nath; Christina Parry; Efren Munoz; Jineta Banerjee; Alexandra J. Scott; Milen Nikolov; Sang Y. Lee
articles_hidden.abstract:
The NF Data Portal (nf.synapse.org) is a free, open-science platform that centralizes data and resources related to neurofibromatosis (NF) and schwannomatosis (SWN), a group of rare genetic tumor predisposition syndromes. The portal hosts a growing collection of NF and SWN multimodal datasets including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and imaging with links to resources such as patient-derived tumor tissue collections, cell lines and preclinical models. The goal of the portal is to provide the broader academic and commercial research community with well-annotated, trusted datasets that can be used in a variety of ways, including asking new scientific questions, benchmarking new methods or tools, and combining datasets across studies. Ultimately, our mission is to accelerate the discovery of treatments and cures for NF and SWN through maximizing the global usability of high-quality data. . 
The NF Data Portal has a cross-institutional backbone of supporters composed of funding organizations, a data coordination center, and a community of clinicians and scientists. Together, this community has developed reusable building blocks for open science, including shared infrastructure, governance frameworks, metadata standards, and a structured data contribution lifecycle. In this publication, we reflect on over a decade of effort to support the data contributor and data user journeys. We share recent platform features and integrations and highlight newly available datasets. 
Whether longtime NF scientists or those encountering this resource for the first time, the NF Data Portal provides access to one of the largest NF datasets available to advance academic research, industry-driven discovery and therapeutic development. For industry users, the portal serves as a strategic translational research asset that supports target validation, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and data-driven decision making, helping to de-risk development programs and inform clinical strategy. As AI-driven analytical methods transform biomedical research, richly annotated, disease-specific datasets like those housed in the NF Data Portal, will be essential raw material for developing and validating new tools and novel treatments.

articles.title: No convincing evidence for a mediated effect of Type D personality on quality of life: A reanalysis of Wang et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using the covariance matrix published by Wang et al., we reexamined the evidence for their proposed mediation framework linking Type D personality to diminished quality of life. We show that the reported associations can be reproduced almost exactly by an alternative latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional sequence assumed in the original study. In this competing account, self-reported Type D personality, perceived stress, psychological distress, and impaired quality of life are conceptualized as observable manifestations of an underlying core self-evaluation construct. The results illustrate the problem of underdetermination in observational research, whereby different theoretical models can account equally well for the same empirical pattern. We therefore argue that greater consideration should be given to alternative model specifications and that correlational findings should be interpreted cautiously when making claims about underlying mechanisms.

articles.title: Hate No More? Assessing an AI-Supported Adaptive Intervention Approach to Address Online Hostility Against Muslim Refugees
articles.authors: Nadine Knab; Anna Luisa Büssow; Melanie Steffens
articles.abstract: Online hate speech fuels anti-Muslim and anti-migrant hostility, yet effective responses remain elusive. We tested whether adaptive interventions – counter-responses tailored to the hostility’s extremity – can foster more open engagement. Across two pre-registered experiments (N = 1,256), participants encountered anti-Muslim content followed by adapted, non-adapted, or no counter-responses (Experiment 1; N = 600) or interacted with an adaptive chatbot (Experiment 2; N = 656). Although no immediate condition differences emerged on primary outcomes, counter-responses produced shifts in openness one week later. In Experiment 1, both adapted and non-adapted comments increased intellectual humility over time and elicited more open, less rigid language than no comment. In Experiment 2, adaptive chatbot responses reduced dichotomous thinking and elicited greater linguistic openness relative to control conditions. These findings suggest that counter-speech can foster openness, but tailoring responses to hostility may offer limited benefits, highlighting both the promise and constraints of adaptive online interventions.

articles.title: Unveiling Conditions for the Dominance of Category-Level Information in Social Evaluations
articles.authors: Mayan Navon; Kate A. Ratliff; Olivier Corneille
articles.abstract: A common assumption in social cognition models is that people tend to form category-based impressions of others, especially when cognitively taxed or unmotivated to individuate their impressions. Recent work (Navon & Bar-Anan, 2023; Navon et al., 2026) tested this classic assumption in highly controlled settings, and both on more and less automatic evaluative measures. The findings challenged the common assumption, indicating that perceivers default to individuating others instead, even in their more automatic evaluations. In the present research, we investigated the enabling conditions required for documenting category dominance. In Experiment 1 (N = 639, Project Implicit participants), we directly communicated category information, while individuating information required integration. We further manipulated processing goals (individual-based versus category-based) and provided salient perceptual cues of group membership. No categorical dominance emerged on a Single-Target IAT, while self-reported evaluations were consistently dominated by individuating information. Experiment 2 (N = 171, Prolific) recruited paid participants and focused solely on category-based impressions. This setting produced a small categorical dominance effect on the ST-IAT and no dominance effect on self-reports. We conclude that categorical dominance in social evaluations is remarkably difficult to document either on less or more automatic evaluations.

articles.title: Reminders of False Information During Corrections Enhance Subsequent Memory in Older and Younger Adults
articles.authors: Aaron Goldman; Ashley M. Leonard; Paige Kemp; Christopher N. Wahlheim
articles.abstract: Exposure to false information may pose risk for older adults’ perceptions of truth due to age-related impairments in associative memory. Corrections with true information paired with reminders of false information can improve memory for true details in younger adults. However, it is unclear whether the same is true in older adults: reminders could impair memory accuracy by increasing the accessibility of false information or improve accuracy by scaffolding more elaborative associative encoding. Two lab-based experiments adjudicated between these possibilities. Younger (Experiment 1: n = 60, Experiment 2: n = 72) and older (Experiment 1: n = 60, Experiment 2: n = 36) adults read true and false headlines in a social media format. False headlines were corrected with true information from fact-checking websites, sometimes after reminders of false information. Participants attempted to recall true information, rated the accuracy of the recalled information, indicated if it was corrected, and if so, attempted to recall false information. Relative to corrections without reminders, corrections with reminders improved memory for true information and reduced intrusions of false information for both age groups. However, older adults recognized corrections with less discriminability and recall of true information was less contingent upon such recognition. Collectively, these findings suggest that older and younger adults used reminders of false information to support associative encoding of content and veracity. However, older adults’ memories may have still lacked episodic associative details that signaled the veracity of headlines, such as whether headlines were corrected.

articles.title: Development of an annotated dataset of persuasion strategies and initial testing of a natural language processing tool to detect persuasion strategies in text
articles.authors: Robert Rhys Thomas; Kate Muir; Ekatarina Kochmar; Adam Joinson; Faye Walker
articles.abstract: In this project, we have worked on the development of a natural-language processing tool to support the automation of persuasive dialogue detection within large corpora of text. The corpus has been generated using a framework for persuasion strategies (Muir et al., 2022) which consists of conversational moves which a persuader will use to achieve their overarching persuasive aim. Seven dominant strategies are identified in this framework: Rapport and liking, Negotiating, Appeals to emotion, Appeals to logic, Appeals to authority, Social proof and Overt persuasion, manipulation, and pressure. This framework was used to annotate the Persuasion for Good corpus (Wang et al. 2019) and we then conducted a series of studies to test whether our model can accurately identify conversations in which attempted persuasion is known to be present, and created a classifier for predicting the probabilities of a given persuasion move being present in any given utterance. We present the initial results of these studies and discuss the implications of using the classifier to identify where both benign and malicious forms of persuasion are taking place in online conversations.

articles.title: Reliance on peripheral vision under divided attention impairs hazard localization in dynamic natural scenes and is not mitigated by attentional cues
articles.authors: Ginnie Wee; Jiali Song; Benjamin Wolfe
articles.abstract: Safe driving requires timely detection of road hazards, yet drivers often engage in secondary tasks that require them to look away from the road, like using phones, resulting in visual distraction. In Experiment 1, we investigated how visual distraction affects gaze strategy during hazard localization, by recording eye movements as licensed drivers located lateralized hazards in dashcam videos while they simultaneously completed a continuous secondary task. Compared to the single-task condition, distraction reduced hazard localization accuracy and slowed response time. Moreover, participants were less likely to respond to non-fixated hazards, suggesting an impaired ability to locate hazards in the visual periphery, even though engaging with the secondary task required them to use peripheral vision to perform the hazard localization task. In Experiment 2, we examined whether attentional cues, in the form of duration-based eyes-off-road (EOR) warnings, reduced missed hazards and encouraged more thorough search of the road scene. We tested two EOR duration thresholds for warnings (1s and 1.5s) but neither condition improved hazard localization compared to the warning absent condition. Across these experiments, higher gaze transition entropy was correlated with improved hazard localization performance, but not the dispersion of fixations, suggesting that scene guidance of eye movements contributes to observers’ ability to locate key objects in the scene. These results suggest that visual distraction substantially impairs observers’ ability to extract information from peripheral vision, and that even highly salient cues may not shift attention and gaze allocation when the distracting task is prioritized.

articles.title: The Public Service Motivation Paradox: Why Highly Motivated Public Servants Are Vulnerable to Psychological Strain
articles.authors: Saut Gracer Sijabat
articles.abstract: Public Service Motivation (PSM) has been seen as a motivational resource that encourages commitment, prosocial behavior, and various positive outcomes in public organizations. However, a growing body of research shows that employees with high PSM are also prone to experiencing burnout, emotional exhaustion, presenteeism, and various forms of psychological distress. These findings raise a theoretical paradox that cannot be fully explained by the PSM literature. This article aims to reconceptualize PSM beyond traditional positive assumptions and develop a conceptual framework that is able to explain the coexistence between high PSM and low employee well-being. Using an integrative conceptual analysis approach, this article synthesizes and critiques the literature on PSM, employee welfare, Job Demands-Resources (JD-R), and Self-Determination Theory (SDT). The results of the analysis resulted in the concept of Public Service Motivation Paradox, which argues that PSM does not directly produce welfare or psychological distress. On the contrary, PSM encourages psychological investment in public services which can subsequently activate a motivational pathway or vulnerability pathway depending on the organizational conditions faced by employees. By integrating JD-R and SDT, this article explains that the paradox arises through the interaction between resource depletion and psychological need frustration. This article contributes by shifting the focus of the PSM literature from outcomes to processes and providing a new theoretical perspective to understand how public service commitment can be a source of well-being as well as psychological vulnerability.

articles.title: Variation in the determinants of semantic decision-making across adulthood
articles.authors: Paul Hoffman; Clementine Figgis; Rachel Gorton; Ruohan Xu
articles.abstract: How do people use semantic knowledge to guide decision-making? Semantic decisions can be affected both by the intrinsic qualities of the concepts being considered and the relationships between them. Age-related change in these factors is rarely studied; yet this can provide valuable insights into how semantic cognition develops across the lifespan. We investigated the factors influencing semantic decisions in 537 adults aged 20–91 years. Participants made two types of verbal semantic decision: global relatedness judgements and feature-specific judgements based on object colour. We predicted accuracy and response time from age, the intrinsic properties of the item being judged, and the strengths of target and distractor relationships on each trial.  Effects of intrinsic properties varied markedly with age. Younger adults made more errors when faced with less frequent and less concrete items, but these effects diminished across adulthood, suggesting that greater experience can reinforce the representation of uncommon and abstract concepts. In contrast, higher semantic diversity impaired performance disproportionately in older people, suggesting that older adults experienced greater difficulty when concepts activated many different associations. Strong but task-irrelevant semantic distractors also led to more errors, particularly among older adults. These findings indicate that the determinants of semantic decision-making shift systematically across adulthood. Younger people have difficulty dealing with infrequent, abstract concepts with which they have limited experience; while advancing age is associated with greater difficulty resolving competition among simultaneously active aspects of meaning. Our data support the view that semantic knowledge accumulates throughout adulthood while goal-directed selection of knowledge declines.

articles.title: Social camouflaging among autistic adolescents in Japan: Diﬀerential associations with aﬃliate stigma reported by mothers and fathers
articles.authors: REIRI NAMURA; Siqing Guan; Aya Taniguchi; Sophia Guan; Fumiyo Oshima
articles.abstract: Autistic adolescents’ use of social camouflaging, defined as strategies used to appear less visibly autistic during social interaction, has increasingly been recognized in previous studies; however, its developmental and family context remains unclear. Affiliate stigma, experienced by family members owing to their association with an autistic individual, and internalized stigma, reflecting the incorporation of negative societal beliefs concerning autism into one’s self-concept, may be relevant correlates. Using an online questionnaire survey of 50 autistic adolescent–mother–father triads, this study examined the associations among parental affiliate stigma, autistic adolescents’ internalized stigma, and social camouflaging, while examining maternal and paternal association patterns. Adolescents reported social camouflaging and internalized stigma, and parents reported affiliate stigma. Path analyses, adjusted for age and autistic traits, indicated that autistic adolescents’ internalized stigma was positively associated with social camouflaging. Both maternal and paternal affiliate stigma were positively associated with adolescents’ internalized stigma in the separate maternal and paternal models and remained independently associated with internalized stigma when modeled simultaneously. The estimated indirect association with social camouflaging was only statistically significant for paternal affiliate stigma in the combined model.

articles.title: Subtractive Epistemology:  Why Psychology Accepts Claims but Cannot Withdraw Them
articles.authors: Tomasz Witkowski
articles.abstract: Psychology has elaborate tools governing the conditions under which a claim enters the corpus of knowledge, and nothing comparable for claims already in it. I show that this is a difference in kind, not of degree, and I explain why. I define the corpus not as an archive of publications but as the set of claims entitled to serve as a premise without renewed justification, and I distinguish the registers granting and revoking that entitlement: research discourse, the publication record, teaching, applied practice, and institutional recognition. I argue that the greater the loss active and established members of the community anticipate from a metascientific reform, the less it is institutionalized, with anticipated rather than incurred cost being decisive. I test this against the fates of reforms rather than of concepts, and I order the existing subtractive tools as a chain of recognition, adjudication, and execution whose last link breaks. What is missing is neither a method nor a tool, but a form in which the result of applying them would be announced, and an actor obliged to announce it. I state the conditions that would render the thesis false.

articles.title: Temporal compression of naturalistic events in episodic memory: Effects of environmental familiarity and action involvement
articles.authors: Bastien Durocher; Nathan Leroy; Arnaud D'Argembeau
articles.abstract: Episodic memories are temporally compressed summaries of past experience, with the degree of compression varying with event characteristics. This study examined how two such characteristics—environmental familiarity and action involvement—influence temporal compression, objective recall content, and subjective memory quality. Across three experiments, participants viewed first-person videos of navigation (walking) in familiar or unfamiliar places, with goal-directed action videos (e.g., buying a notebook) also included in two of the experiments. Participants then mentally replayed each video to derive a compression measure, alongside subjective ratings and recall descriptions. Action involvement consistently reduced compression and enriched both subjective and objective aspects of remembering. Environmental familiarity effects on compression were context-dependent: absent when videos were recalled immediately after viewing (Experiment 1), present — with unfamiliar videos remembered in less compressed form — when familiarity was blocked across separate lists (Experiment 2), and eliminated when familiar and unfamiliar videos were mixed within the same lists (Experiment 3). Familiar videos were nonetheless consistently rated as more detailed and easier to remember, independent of list composition. Overall, environmental familiarity shaped the subjective experience of remembering without altering objective recall content, revealing a partial dissociation between subjective and objective memory measures, whereas action involvement consistently benefited both, underscoring the structuring role of actions in event memory. These results are discussed in relation to schema-based encoding, working-memory resource, and scene-construction accounts of temporal compression.

articles.title: What are the self-harm and suicide-related social media experiences of LGBTQ+ young people?  A national survey comparing LGBTQ+ and non-LGBTQ+ young Australians
articles.authors: Charlie Cooper; Louise La Sala; Pamela Patrick; lefteris patlamazoglou; Bridget Kenny; Caroline X. Gao; Michelle Lamblin; Angela Nicholas; Matthew Spittal; Ann John
articles.abstract: LGBTQ+ young people are disproportionately affected by self-harm and suicide and are active social media users, yet little is known about their suicide-related online experiences. We analysed data from a quota-sampled survey of Australian social media users aged 15–25 (N = 885; LGBTQ+ n = 249). Compared with their non-LGBTQ+ peers, LGBTQ+ youth had over fourfold higher odds of exposure to self-harm and suicide-related content, and elevated odds of creating such content and seeking help on social media. More LGBTQ+ youth reported worsened mood and self-harm following exposure. These findings suggest that engagement-driven algorithms may create a feedback loop in which help-seeking amplifies harmful exposure. Enforceable platform accountability frameworks that reduce harmful exposure without limiting support pathways are needed.

articles.title: How the voice mediates speaker-listener emotional understanding of happiness
articles.authors: Maël Mauchand; Leonardo Ceravolo; Didier Grandjean
articles.abstract: In everyday communication, there is no formal way to guarantee that the emotions we attribute to our interlocutor’s voice truly reflect their internal state. Whereas most research on emotion communication involves either reporting acoustic correlates of emotion categories or assessing perceptual responses to specific stimuli, this study aimed to establish a direct relationship between speaker expression and listener perception. Thirty-three participants expressed and perceived emotional voices in a chained design: each participant produced pseudo-words with happy and neutral prosodies, listened to their own productions, and listened to the productions of the participant before them twice. Every trial included a happiness rating, such that each pseudoword was evaluated by the speaker as they spoke (production rating) and as they heard themselves again (self-perception rating), as well as the next listener hearing them for the first time (other-perception rating) and after a first exposure (other-reperception rating). Acoustic analyses of the vocal productions revealed variable but relatively consistent prosodic patterns in expressing happiness. Perceptual-acoustic analyses of the happiness ratings revealed that happiness perception is not only categorically accurate but also reflect significant speaker-listener alignment, dependent on speaker’s expressive style and listener’s familiarity. These results provide an individual-based, lens model account of vocal emotion, capturing aspects of affective communication seldom reported in traditional emotion research.

articles.title: Portable Brain Vital Sign Changes Following Resilience Training in First Responders
articles.authors: William Tanner Creel; Eric D. Kirby; Ryan CN D’Arcy; Kevin Smith; Susan Farren; Tori R Van Dyk
articles.abstract:
Objective:
First responders are routinely exposed to chronic occupational stress and may underreport psychological strain due to stigma and confidentiality concerns. Objective neurophysiological measures can provide useful adjunctive markers of intervention-related neurocognitive change in this population. The present study evaluated whether participation in a neuroscience-informed resilience training program was associated with measurable changes in event-related potentials (ERPs), providing objective evidence of the program’s real-world impact. 

Methods:
A retrospective pre-post design was used to analyze ERPs from 57 first responders who completed a three-day proactive resilience training program. ERPs were acquired using a brain vital sign framework, which included amplitude and latency metrics for the N100, P300, and N400 responses. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated pre-post changes while adjusting for age and sex, with false discovery rate correction applied across outcomes.

Results:
Significant pre-post changes were observed for N400 latency, alongside a significant increase in N400 amplitude following the intervention. N400 latency decreased (β = -35.57 ms, q = .002) and N400 amplitude increased (β = 0.70, q < .001). No significant changes were observed for N100 or P300 responses following correction.

Conclusions:
First responders demonstrated selective modulation of N400 indices following resilience training, which may reflect changes in higher-order cognitive processing speed and contextual integration. Findings provide preliminary evidence of intervention-associated neurophysiological change.

Significance:
There is a pressing need for translational evidence demonstrating that real-world training programs produce objective impact. Taking advantage of the utility of ERPs as sensitive neurophysiological measures, the present findings highlight the potential value of resilience training for modulating neurocognitive processing in high-stress occupational populations

articles.title: Differential Influences of Self-Disclosure and Recent Exposure on Listener Autonomic Reactions to Stuttering
articles.authors: David Jenson; Edward C. Brown; David Thornton
articles.abstract:
Purpose:  The current study used autonomic responses (heart rate, skin conductance) as measures of implicit reactions to stuttering to determine whether previous reports of more positive listener reactions to disclosed stuttering are mirrored in autonomic reactions.

Method:  Participants (N = 48) viewed videos of non-stuttered speech as well as stuttered speech preceded by either a neutral statement, an informational self-disclosure, or an apologetic self-disclosure.  Participants completed behavioral ratings (semantic differential rating scales and the Self-Assessment Manikin) following each video, with heart rate and skin conductance recorded throughout.

Results:  Autonomic signals did not differ across disclosure conditions, but demonstrated a clear order effect.  The first presentation of stuttering elicited a large heart rate deceleration and increased skin conductance while successive stuttering presentations elicited smaller heart rate decelerations and a reduction in skin conductance.  Explicit reactions were more negative for stuttered compared to non-stuttered speech, with stuttering preceded by informational disclosure rated as more soothing than undisclosed stuttering or apologetically disclosed stuttering.

Conclusion:  Explicit reactions to stuttering may be influenced by disclosure, while implicit autonomic reactions to stuttering are sensitive to recent stuttering exposure rather than disclosure.  Findings are interpreted to suggest that disclosure and repeated exposure to stuttering may influence distinct channels of listener reactions.

articles.title: “You have to make it on your own:” A person-centered narrative analysis of neoliberal capitalist values in adolescent identity experiences
articles.authors: Margaux Schoofs; Reitske Meganck; Liesbeth Taels; Kate C. McLean; Melissa Miléna De Smet
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Neoliberal capitalist ideals are omnipresent today and have important consequences for how adolescents develop an identity. However, we know little about the ways in which adolescents engage with these ideals and the neoliberal capitalist structures they are subjected to. Therefore, in this study we aim to investigate how adolescents construct their narrative identities within and throughout the socio-cultural framework of neoliberal capitalism.  
Method: To this end, we conducted a person-centered narrative analysis of in-depth interviews with four Flemish adolescents: Marie (16, girl), Alex (16, boy), Tim (14, boy), and Jason (17, boy). Our participants were purposefully selected out of a sample of fourteen. 
Results: Most notable in the analysis of our study was the pattern of individual control the adolescents used, constructing their personal narratives in terms of being the master of themselves, their context, and their futures. The participants were the main characters ruling everything, while the people surrounding them remained diffuse side characters, little differentiated, usually reduced to one characteristic, trait, or flaw.
Conclusions: Our analysis argues for the consideration of this narrative pattern when conceptualizing adolescent development, wellbeing, and meaning making. Additionally, we highlight the central role parents play in the adolescents’ engagements with the pattern of individual control.

articles.title: Refbank: an open repository of iterated reference game data
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Jess Mankewitz; Fiona Feng; Benji Fernandez; Ryder Fried; Michael C. Frank; Robert Hawkins
articles.abstract: Language users flexibly produce and interpret language in context, and over time modulate their language use to convey meanings with greater accuracy and efficiency. Adaptive language use is often studied using iterated reference games, which represent a controlled way of studying how people communicate in the absence of codified labels, and how conventionalised labels form over repeated reference to the same targets. While iterated reference games are a common paradigm, the research questions, pre-processing, and analytic approaches differ across papers so their results are challenging to synthesise using meta-analysis. Here, we present Refbank, a harmonised repository of iterated reference game data from 20 different papers, enabling quantitative synthesis in novel and larger-scale analyses. We conduct five mega-analyses that shed light on the robustness and variability of convention formation under different experimental settings. Refbank also has potential future uses for targeted experiment design, computational modelling, and language model evaluation. These directions demonstrate the utility of reusing data from iterated reference games, and we invite contributions of additional datasets to Refbank.

articles.title: Tests of measurement invariance for nine relationship relevant scales across straight, gay/lesbian, and bisexual individuals
articles.authors: Hannah S Elizabeth; Margaret Clark
articles.abstract: Utilizing a data set including roughly equal numbers of straight, gay/lesbian, and bisexual individuals, we tested the measurement invariance of nine relationship relevant measures—relationship quality (Fletcher et al., 2000), sexual satisfaction (Park & MacDonald, 2022), social comparison orientation (Gibbons & Buunk, 1999), social support (Mitchell et al., 2003 and Cutrona & Russell, 1987), homophily (McCroskey et al, 1975), attachment (Fraley et al., 2000), relationship status satisfaction (Lehmann et al., 2015) and self-expansion (Hughes et al., 2020). When justified based on the measurement invariance results, we conducted tests for latent mean differences. Our results lead us to recommend researchers studying varying sexual orientations utilize Fletcher et al. (2000), Park & MacDonald (2022), Mitchell et al. (2003) and Lehmann et al. (2015). Two others—McCroskey et al., 2011 and Fraley et al., 2000—required modifications before attaining scalar invariance. Gibbons & Buunk, 1999 showed evidence of good fit with the original model, but only partial invariance across sexuality groups. We urge caution with this measure. We do not recommend use of the final two measures: Cutrona & Russell and Hughes et al, 2020. Given the exploratory nature of the work, our results should be both used with caution and replicated.

articles.title: Learner-directed registers in foreign word learning
articles.authors: Katie Von Holzen
articles.abstract: In comparison to speech directed to native adult speakers (native-directed speech; NDS), speech directed to non-native speakers of a language (non-native-directed speech; NNDS) has altered acoustic-prosodic characteristics, such as a slower speech rate, a higher fundamental frequency, greater pitch variation, and vowel hyperarticulation. Together with infant-directed speech (IDS) which is used with infants, these learner-directed registers have been proposed to serve a didactic purpose in language learning (Uther et al. 2007). Despite decades of research on IDS, the facilitatory role of speech modifications in foreign language acquisition has received little attention, with one study to-date showing that NNDS facilitates word learning in foreign language learners (Piazza et al. 2023). Using the word learning paradigm of Golinkoff and Alioto (1995), German-speaking adults with no prior experience learning Mandarin Chinese were familiarized with 10 words in Mandarin Chinese and then tested on their recognition. In a between-subjects design, the familiarization phase was produced using either a NDS, NNDS, or IDS register. Participants’ exhibited learning in all three conditions and there was no difference in accuracy between conditions. Taken together, these results suggest that facilitation for learner-directed registers may not be generalizable to all learning contexts.

articles.title: Testing the Alliance and Cognitive Change as Simultaneous Processes of Change in Cognitive Therapy for Anxiety
articles.authors: Alexandra Kaelin Barnhill; Madeline Kushner; Doug Terrill; Matthew W. Southward
articles.abstract: Researchers have proposed that both a strong working alliance and cognitive change are key processes of change in cognitive therapy for emotional disorders. Schmidt et al. (2019) demonstrated that within-person cognitive change occurring between sessions mediated the relation between within-person cognitive change in the previous session and subsequent depression improvement. We conducted a conceptual replication and extension of Schmidt et al. (2019) in a sample of adults with elevated anxiety (N = 200; Mage = 32.1; 78% female, 80% White, 73% heterosexual) who completed self-report measures before and after four sessions of cognitive therapy. Using dynamic structural equation modeling, we replicated Schmidt et al.’s (2019) results that between-session cognitive change (CC-S) mediated the relation between in-session cognitive change (CC-I) and depression improvement (ODSIS; B = –.16, p < .01) and extended them to improvements in anxiety (OASIS; B = –.18, p < .01). We also found that between-session cognitive change mediated the relation between the working alliance (WAI-SR) and anxiety and depression improvement (Bs: –.12 - –.11, ps < .01). The indirect effects involving cognitive change did not significantly differ from those involving the total alliance and agreement on the tasks of therapy, ps > .15, but were stronger than those involving agreement on the goals of therapy and the therapeutic bond, ps < .03. Both the alliance and cognitive change may be key processes of change, albeit at different steps in the overall pathway, in cognitive therapy for emotional disorders.

articles.title: Altered adaptive mentalization in autistic adults
articles.authors: Niklas Bürgi; Arkady Konovalov; Caroline Biegel; Tania Villar de Araujo; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff
articles.abstract: Autism has long been linked to difficulties in understanding others’ mental states. However, what specific neuro-cognitive mechanisms underlie these mentalization difficulties remains poorly understood. Here, we show that a key determinant of behavioral difficulties is reduced adaptation to others’ idiosyncratic ways of reasoning. We demonstrate this with computational modelling and functional magnetic resonance imaging in 89 adults (43 autistic and 46 neurotypical) who played repeated interactive games, following a pre-registered analysis plan. As predicted, we found reduced behavioral performance in autistic participants, which our model attributed to a decreased ability to adapt to others’ changing behavioral strategies. Neurally, the autistic group showed no consistent regional activation differences but reduced and less precise expression of a previously identified multivariate signature of adaptive mentalization, suggesting distributed rather than localized functional changes in the neural systems supporting dynamic social reasoning. Our approach provides a mechanistic account of mentalizing difficulties in autism and may aid in its assessment and diagnosis.

articles.title: Navigating Dynamic Risks: Neural Adaptation in Sequential Decision-Making
articles.authors: Corinna Lorenz; Nicola Kristina Ferdinand
articles.abstract:
Real-world risk-taking unfolds through sequences of decisions where stakes escalate incrementally. Yet most
ERP research examines isolated outcomes, leaving neural adaptation to accumulating risk poorly understood. We developed an ERP-adapted Columbia Card Task enabling precise temporal analysis of feedback processing across consecutive outcomes, systematically manipulating gain amounts, loss amounts, and loss
probability while recording EEG in 25 participants. We measured early outcome detection via the feedback-related negativity (FRN) and reward positivity (RewP) and later evaluative processing via the P3b. All three components showed systematic adaptation with component-specific sensitivities to risk parameters.
The FRN exhibited context-dependent shifts between habituation and sensitization: valence differentiation
was amplified under conditions where monitoring was most critical — when potential gains were modest or
losses severe. The RewP showed stake-dependent valence differentiation, with larger loss amounts enhancing the distinction between positive and negative outcomes and increasing sensitivity to relative outcome valence within the current risk context. The P3b consistently prioritized negative outcomes, with sustained attentional resources amplifying under higher stakes. Exploratory analyses revealed fundamentally opposing temporal adaptation strategies as a function of individual risk propensity, emerging specifically under high-stakes conditions. Risk-prone individuals showed progressive sensitization to negative outcomes alongside maintained positive outcome evaluation; risk-averse individuals showed the inverse pattern. Critically, both groups achieved equivalent task performance, suggesting these divergent neural signatures reflect strategic regulatory approaches rather than processing deficits. These findings advance understanding of how the brain navigates dynamic risk environments and when adaptive risk-taking may transition toward maladaptive patterns.

articles.title: Examining the Benefits of Spaced Retrieval Practice on Transfer and the Student Experience in the Classroom
articles.authors: Varun Ramgopal; Greta M. Fastrich; Philip Anthony Higham; Ariana Modirrousta-Galian; Mansi Pattni; Rosalind Potts; Tina Seabrooke
articles.abstract:
Spaced retrieval practice is a learning strategy whereby information is retrieved multiple times with each retrieval attempt separated by a time gap. We conducted a semester-long classroom intervention to investigate the benefits of spaced retrieval practice on memory and transfer. Each week, students engaged in three, spaced learning practice sessions (LPSs) during which they either answered multiple-choice (MC) questions about that week’s course content (retrieval practice) or were shown the MC questions with the correct answer selected (restudy). Three weeks after the last LPS, participants completed a final MC test comprising (1) repeated questions from the LPSs, (2) transfer questions that had the same answer options as corresponding LPS questions and queried related topics, but had different correct answers, or (3) new questions about lecture content.  A typical retrieval practice effect was observed for repeated questions (retrieval > restudy). Although we did not observe a transfer effect on overall final test accuracy (related = new), further exploratory analyses that used purer measures of transfer revealed evidence of both positive and negative transfer. Furthermore, retrieval practice (vs. restudying) contributed to an enhanced student experience (greater sense of mastery, motivation, and attentional control, and reduced anxiety). 

Keywords: spaced learning, retrieval practice, transfer, testing effect, spaced retrieval practice

articles.title: Eco-Anxiety and Neoliberal Orientation: A latent class analysis
articles.authors: Rilary Barroso; Maria Ildenice da Silva; Caio Maximino
articles.abstract: The climate crisis has given rise to eco‑anxiety, yet the interplay between its distinct psychological facets and ideological orientations such as neoliberalism remains empirically underexplored. This study integrated network analysis and latent class analysis (LCA) to examine the construct validity of the Climate Anxiety Scale (CAS) and the Eco‑Anxiety Scale (HEAS‑13), and to identify how neoliberal orientation (NOQ‑S) moderates profiles of eco‑distress. The network analysis confirmed convergent validity between the CAS and HEAS‑13 through a shared cognitive‑ruminative core, while revealing their complementary specificity: the CAS uniquely anchored behavioral engagement and moral guilt, whereas the HEAS‑13 specifically captured personal helplessness and inefficacy. Crucially, neoliberal orientation did not uniformly suppress eco‑anxiety; rather, it exhibited selective negative edges with behavioral engagement and perceived personal efficacy, while leaving cognitive‑emotional rumination relatively intact. The LCA identified four distinct profiles: (1) low neoliberalism with adaptive eco‑anxiety; (2) high neoliberalism with maladaptive, ruminative eco‑anxiety; (3) high neoliberalism with low eco‑anxiety; and (4) low neoliberalism with low eco‑anxiety. The network architecture provides a mechanistic explanation for these latent profiles, demonstrating that high neoliberal orientation can co‑exist with maladaptive eco‑anxiety when ideological suppression specifically targets action and efficacy pathways rather than the core distress itself. These findings robustly validate the CAS and HEAS‑13 as complementary measures and position neoliberal ideology as a critical psychological moderator that decouples anxious arousal from pro‑environmental engagement, with important implications for activism and climate communication.

articles.title: Are We Forgetting Something? Two of the Most Effective Learning Strategies Are Not Explained in Teacher-Education Materials
articles.authors: Magnus Ingebrigtsen; Vetle Lars Wisløff Sandring; Jarle Bastesen; Tove Irene Dahl; Rannveig Grøm Sæle
articles.abstract: Educational reforms often emphasize that students should learn to learn and use good learning strategies. Spaced repetition and retrieval practice are two effective and well-documented strategies that reliably improve both comprehension, retention, and knowledge transfer. They can also increase interest and reduce test anxiety, making them especially relevant for teachers. However, many learners misunderstand or underutilize these strategies, and research indicates they are underrepresented in teacher education curricula. To investigate this, we analyzed assigned readings in Norway’s largest postgraduate teacher training programs (PPU-A). Using zero-shot text classification, we identified 992 excerpts likely to address repetition or retrieval. Two coders then evaluated whether these excerpts contained accurate explanations or examples. We found no complete explanations of either strategy. Some excerpts provided clear examples, but most were incomplete or ambiguous. This suggests that two fundamental cognitive strategies with clear educational relevance are being overlooked or misconceived in teacher education curricula.

articles.title: Beyond Perceptual Expertise: Identity and Affect Pathways to Other-Race Recognition
articles.authors: Li Shan Joy Tong; Sacha Epskamp; Daniel DongWon Oh
articles.abstract: Other-race recognition difficulties contribute to wrongful convictions and discourage interracial integration. These difficulties are typically attributed to limited perceptual expertise with other-race faces and a tendency to categorise others by race rather than as individuals. Using theory-driven variable selection and data-driven network modelling, we show that other-race recognition is not just perceptual; it is also shaped by identity and affect. Participants (N = 512) completed face recognition tasks, and measures of personality, interracial contact, ethnic-racial attitudes and identity, and emotion. Hostility impairs other-race recognition,  and is itself heightened by anti-dominant ethnic-racial identity, whereas ethnic-racial awareness and intergroup affection improve recognition. Individuating experiences mattered more than contact quantity. By focusing on personal, rather than group-based, construals of race, this study reframes other-race recognition as shaped by intergroup affect and ethnic-racial identity, not perceptual or socio-cognitive processes alone. Interventions targeting hostility and ethnic-racial identity may offer promising avenues for improving other-race recognition.

articles.title: The Future of Educational Psychology: Between Vision and Dystopia
articles.authors: Julia Moeller; Carla Geiger; Henrik Saalbach
articles.abstract:
This study examined trends in the future development of educational psychology using a mixed-methods approach. First, a scoping review identified articles containing explicit statements about the future of educational psychology, from which categories of anticipated developments were derived. Second, experts in educational psychology completed an online survey with open-ended questions on expectations, hopes, and best- and worst-case scenarios for the field’s future, and rated 84 statements—derived from the scoping review—on their perceived probability of occurring. ChatGPT completed the same survey. Articles from the scoping review and experts’ open-ended responses were analyzed using natural language processing techniques (e.g., sentiment analysis, word clouds) alongside qualitative categorization.
The findings revealed a wide range of predictions, spanning from utopian to dystopian scenarios. Utopian visions emphasized interdisciplinary, multimethod, and evidence-based research with strong societal and political impact, leveraging advanced technologies to support personalized learning as well as mental health and social-emotional development. Dystopian scenarios expressed concern that educational psychology and quality education could become marginalized, politically constrained, inaccessible to many learners, or replaced by automated systems. Experts also identified concrete action points aimed at fostering desirable developments and preventing unfavorable futures.

articles.title: Indeterminate Interpretation and Transportation Experiences in Text Comprehension
articles.authors: Miho Fuyama
articles.abstract: Studies in hermeneutics and on reading and art theories have indicated that the indeterminacy of readers' interpretations and texts enhances their immersion and aesthetic experiences. This study classifies the types of indeterminacy and investigates the relationship between indeterminacy and readers' transportation states. The framework of quantum cognition using quantum (non-commutative) probability theory is employed to model the indeterminacy related to emergent interpretations, and test the relationship between an order effect that indicates this type of indeterminacy and the transportation states of readers. With a sample size of 3,027 participants, the study uses a Japanese short story as its material. Results reveal that the number of paragraphs with significant order effects in the high-transportation group is larger than that in the low-transportation group, suggesting a relationship between indeterminacy and transportation state. This result also contributes to a discussion on two types in cognitions of a sense of reality: the reading and virtual reality types.

articles.title: Conflict, not category: What the pupil tracks in face pareidolia
articles.authors: Amanda K Robinson; Jing Liang; Blake William Saurels; Jessica Taubert
articles.abstract: Illusory faces, the faces people see in inanimate objects, share the low-level image statistics of the objects they are made of while, nonetheless, being perceived as faces. Neural representations of illusory faces shift from face-like to object-like within roughly 200 ms, and observers explicitly categorise them as objects, yet the illusion remains compelling. We asked whether the pupil, a peripheral index of both light and arousal, is sensitive to this dual identity. Forty participants viewed sequences of human faces, illusory faces in objects, and matched non-face objects (100 images each) while performing an orthogonal task at fixation. Human faces and objects both evoked pupil constriction, whereas illusory faces produced dilation beginning at approximately 350 ms. Thus, rather than falling between faces and objects or resembling either category, illusory faces elicited a qualitatively different pupil response. This dissociation remained after controlling for luminance and emotional valence, despite luminance being the strongest determinant of pupil size. Critically, within the illusory images, the dilation scaled with independent measures of the strength of the face percept, including face-likeness and the probability of categorisation as a face, and did not diminish across repeated presentations. These findings are consistent with the pupil tracking the conflict between the object and face interpretations, rather than stimulus category per se.  They suggest that although neural representations quickly settle on an object's veridical identity, the competing illusory face interpretation persists, revealing a physiological signature of the conflicting perceptual identities that define face pareidolia.

articles.title: Cross-cultural and Indigenous perspectives on music and social bonding
articles.authors: Danya Vivianne Pavlovich; Patricia Opondo; Juan David Leongómez; Yuto Ozaki; Zixuan Jia; Suzanne Purdy; Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. Critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on new data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators (“Many Voices”), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

articles.title: Comment on Boger & Firestone (2026): Perceiving animacy in ‘identical’ images
articles.authors: Surya Gayet
articles.abstract: Boger and Firestone (2026) use a novel set of hybrid stimuli whose identity changes with rotation. They find that change-detection is easier when such images cross the animate-inanimate boundary, and that targets are found faster among distractors of the opposite animacy, despite these objects being constituted of the same pixel-by-pixel content. These results are taken as evidence that animacy influences visual cognition independently of its lower-level visual correlates. Here, I challenge this inference on two grounds. First, rotation preserves global image statistics but changes the positions and orientations of local features in a retinotopic, anisotropic visual system. Second, findings obtained with a small set of deliberately ambiguous images do not establish the mechanisms of ordinary object recognition. Visual anagrams are ingenious stimuli, but their usefulness for isolating animacy from its visual correlates remains limited.

articles.title: Social Media as a Context of Narrative Identity Development: A Reflexive Thematic Analysis Study
articles.authors: Irena Stojković; Marijana Veselinović; Božidar Filipović
articles.abstract: In the present study, we aimed to understand how emerging adults experience their social media engagement and how these experiences may be relevant to narrative identity construction from the perspective of the process model of narrative identity development (McLean et al., 2007). Individual semi-structured interviews with 27 emerging adults (19 females, 8 males) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Three themes were developed: Social media as a space for meaningful communication, Online identity as a selective presentation of self, and Curating the social media profile through self-reflection. The first theme captures self-expression, exchange of perspectives, and social recognition through social media. The second refers to perceptions of online self-presentation as selective and providing a partial, and at times misleading, representation of the person. The third describes the process of editing one’s profile through evaluating whether posts accurately reflect one’s current identity. Taken together, these themes suggest that social media can provide a context for situated storytelling and narrative identity construction, offering opportunities for meaningful communication while also potentially constraining self-expression and autobiographical reasoning, depending on how individuals engage with these platforms.

articles.title: The right visual field advantage in crowding is specific to letters
articles.authors: Alex L. White; Nicole Oppenheimer; Anishka Yerabothu
articles.abstract: Visual crowding is the impairment to object recognition caused by similar objects that are too close to the target. Although crowding occurs in many contexts, it is not clear whether the underlying mechanisms are the same for all stimulus categories. One clue is that crowding is sometimes less severe in the right visual hemifield than in the left. However, this hemifield asymmetry has emerged most often in letter identification tasks. Here we investigated whether the hemifield asymmetry is a general attribute of crowding or specific to identifying familiar letters. In three experiments, we precisely measured crowding distances (the spacing between targets and flankers required to reach a threshold level of accuracy) in each hemifield for several types of stimuli: Latin letters, pseudo-letters with matched visual features, Landolt squares, and face icons. For letters only, crowding distances were significantly smaller in the right visual field than in the left. This asymmetry was larger for letters than for all other stimulus types. The asymmetry for letters persisted even when the target letter was flanked by unfamiliar pseudo-letters, demonstrating that it is not simply an advantage for processing strings of letters. Two other findings support stimulus-specific mechanisms: the patterns of flanker substitution errors and across-participant correlations in crowding distances. We propose that reading experience strengthens connections between left-hemisphere language areas and left-hemisphere visual cortex, leading to specific letter-processing mechanisms with more precise spatial tuning in the right visual hemifield.

articles.title: Not just for play: fNIRS reveals complex linguistic, perceptual, and sociopragmatic functions of Japanese ideophones
articles.authors: Bonnie McLean; Kimi Akita; Dan P Dewey
articles.abstract: This study investigates the neural processing of Japanese ideophones (expressive words depicting sound, movement, texture, taste, or emotion) compared to verbs and adjectives matched on semantic measures of perceptual strength and multimodality. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), we recorded brain activity while participants listened to ideophones and matched non-ideophones (verbs and adjectives) with meanings spanning five sensory categories: visual, auditory, haptic, gustatory, and interoceptive. General linear model analyses revealed significant differences between brain activity during the processing of ideophones compared to words of other classes, with ideophones eliciting broader activation in occipital, prefrontal, and parietal regions—areas associated with visualization, higher level thinking, and integrative cognition. Principal component analysis further revealed that patterns of neurological activation across sensory categories are different for ideophones than for non-ideophones: compared to non-ideophones, ideophones activated a shared multisensory network of channels with extensive cross-modal coactivation and strong internal coherence. The findings provide new insights into how semiotic distinctions influence processing, and underscore how ideophones—once dismissed as marginal embellishments or ‘playthings’—are perfectly honed tools for a variety of complex linguistic and social functions, by virtue of their depictive natures and the special connections to sensori-affective systems this affords them.

articles.title: Of Break-Ups and New Beginnings - Subjective Event Perceptions in Adult Attachment Dynamics During Relationship Transitions
articles.authors: Alex Traut; Fabian Gander; Rebekka Weidmann; William J. Chopik; Alexander Grob
articles.abstract:
Attachment orientations are theorized to change in response to significant
interpersonal life events. However, empirical findings remain mixed. Moreover, the role of
subjective event perceptions—though emphasized in personality research—has been largely
been neglected in research on attachment development. In a longitudinal study spanning 7
waves over 2.5 years, we examined how romantic relationship transitions—entering or ending
a committed relationship—predict changes in attachment anxiety and avoidance, and whether
these effects are moderated by subjective event perceptions. We analyzed data of N = 1,717
participants (69.6% women aged 18-40, M = 26.5 years) who were single (52%) or in a
partnership (48%) at the beginning of the study. Using multilevel piecewise modeling, we
distinguished selection, anticipation, and socialization effects. Avoidant individuals were less
likely to enter new relationships (selection effect), and avoidance declined prior to partnering
(anticipation effect). Both anxiety and avoidance shifted in response to transitions
(socialization effects): anxiety decreased after partnering and increased after separation, while
avoidance showed a temporary decrease post-separation followed by a gradual increase.
These shifts mirrored average differences between partnered and single individuals,
suggesting rapid adaptation to new social roles. Subjective perceptions of the events (e.g.,
valence, social status decrease, predictability) showed limited moderation effects. Overall,
findings underscore the importance of social role transitions in shaping attachment processes,
while suggesting that subjective evaluations may have a more nuanced role than previously
assumed. These results contribute to personality theory by clarifying the contextual and
experiential mechanisms underlying intraindividual change in attachment insecurity.

articles.title: Identifying the active ingredients of a behavioral activation-based digital single-session intervention
articles.authors: Arka Ghosh; Benjamin Kaveladze; Jessica L. Schleider
articles.abstract: Digital single-session interventions (SSIs) have been shown to be effective in reducing myriad mental health conditions. However, it is unclear which components of SSIs drive their therapeutic effects. In this study, we divided a well-evaluated behavioral activation-based SSI into three candidate components—PSYCHOEDUCATION, TESTIMONIALS, and ACTION PLAN—each hypothesized to have independent therapeutic value. We conducted a 23 factorial experiment (N=889) to evaluate effects of the individual components on depressive symptoms. Our results showed that only the ACTION PLAN candidate component had a significant effect on depressive symptoms at 2-week (d=−0.18) and 8-week (d=−0.12) follow-ups. Additionally, user’s perceptions of the intervention’s credibility and their expectations of improvement were significantly associated with a reduction in depressive symptoms at both time points. Our findings offer a more nuanced understanding of which elements within digital SSIs may drive their therapeutic benefits.

articles.title: Alternative interpretations of the association between interparental conflict and adolescent online flaming: A reanalysis of Zeng et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Using the covariance matrix reported by Zeng et al., we reassess the evidence supporting their proposed mediation model linking interparental conflict to adolescent online flaming. We demonstrate that the observed relationships can be reproduced with high precision by an alternative latent variable model that does not require the sequence of influence suggested in the original article. In this alternative account, adolescent-reported interparental conflict, psychological stress, online disinhibition, and online flaming are viewed as manifestations of broader underlying tendencies related to general disinhibition. The findings illustrate the problem of model underdetermination in observational research, whereby distinct theoretical explanations may fit the same empirical data. We therefore recommend greater attention to competing model specifications and caution when interpreting correlational findings as evidence for specific influencing mechanisms.

articles.title: Designing for Human Flourishing: A Sociotechnical Framework for AI Chatbots
articles.authors: Louis Tay; Karina Vold; Gloria Liou; Harsh Kumar; Daniel Harris; Ashton Anderson
articles.abstract: The rapid adoption of AI chatbots - ranging from purpose-built systems to general-purpose large language models (LLMs) - for supporting human well-being and broader human flourishing requires an integrative interdisciplinary framework. In this article, we advance a sociotechnical framework for designing AI chatbots that support human flourishing, synthesizing four essential disciplinary perspectives (philosophical, behavioral, interactional, and technical) and articulating how their interplay shapes both the promises and risks of AI-based support. Central to our framework is the identification of two fundamental tensions that structure the design and evaluation of such systems: the temporal (i.e., immediate vs. longer-term benefits) and self-community (i.e., individual vs. collective outcomes) tensions. By making these tensions explicit, the framework offers an integrative lens for organizing disparate literatures on AI and human flourishing, generating novel hypotheses about system design and its effects on individual users and society more broadly.  The framework guides both developers seeking to align AI system objectives with human values and policymakers governing the deployment of AI in mental health, education, and social welfare. We advance the field by equipping researchers, practitioners, and policymakers with a roadmap for the responsible design and regulation of AI chatbots that enable, rather than diminish, human flourishing.

articles.title: Too Tired to be Honest? The Role of Mental Fatigue in Dishonesty
articles.authors: Mara Bialas; Daniela Becker; Wolter Pieters; Maarten Alex Sander Boksem; Erik Bijleveld
articles.abstract:
Mental Fatigue, a feeling of exhaustion after prolonged mental effort, could affect when people decide to be honest or dishonest. Thus far, research has put forward two accounts that could explain how fatigue affects the choice to be dishonest: the self-interest overriding and the moral default account. In this study, we tested which of the two accounts people’s propensity to be dishonest or honest aligns more with. Although our manipulation did not yield the anticipated differences in fatigue, we can still draw tentative conclusions about the observed differences in cheating: higher fatigue levels, regardless of condition, are associated with less cheating, which is somewhat more consistent with the self-interest-overriding account. Moreover, within- and between-person fatigue effects showed that within-subjects higher-than-usual fatigue was associated with fewer cheating choices. We advise future fatigue research to focus on how decisions about dishonesty are made, rather than on the outcome of those decisions.
Keywords: Mental Fatigue, Decision Making, Dishonesty, Moral Default

articles.title: The Intellectual Justice Scale: Measuring How Fairly People Engage With Knowledge
articles.authors: Yara Daamen; Vlasta Sikimić; Daniel Lakens
articles.abstract: Intellectual justice, the disposition to engage fairly with knowledge and those who produce it, has received growing attention in philosophy and education, yet no validated self-report measure exists. We developed and validated the Intellectual Justice Scale (IJS), a 9-item measure with three factors (Testimonial Justice, Hermeneutical Justice, and Intellectual Action) grounded in Fricker’s framework of intellectual injustice. An initial item pool was refined through expert review and pilot testing. In Study 1 (N = 404), exploratory factor analysis supported a three-factor structure, with independent statistical and conceptual item selection converging on the same nine items. In Study 2 (N = 401), confirmatory factor analysis supported good model fit, and the IJS showed expected associations with intellectual humility, personality traits, and social justice attitudes while remaining empirically distinguishable from each. These findings offer the first validated self-report measure of intellectual justice attitudes, providing researchers with a tool to study individual differences.

articles.title: No evidence for Nonconscious Goal Pursuit in Novel Environments: A Replication of Eitam et al.’s (2008) Experiment 2
articles.authors: Jason M. Prenoveau; Matthew W Kirkhart
articles.abstract: In two experiments, Eitam, Hassin, and Schul (2008) found evidence that priming of nonconscious goal pursuit could extend beyond reproductions of past associations and facilitate novel learning, specifically implicit learning. Given the implications of such findings and dearth of subsequent investigations of this phenomenon, we conducted a direct replication of their second experiment using materials graciously shared by the original authors. Despite using a sample size that provided .80 power to detect the original effect size, we failed to find evidence that priming of nonconscious goal pursuit facilitated implicit learning. Our replication was conducted as part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) and study preregistration, materials, and data are available online (https://osf.io/edcr7).

articles.title: Positive Affect is Associated with Interactive Social Media Use: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Evelyn Alice Halliday Murray; Daniel Shaw; Jisun Kim; Andrew Jones; Charlotte Rebecca Pennington
articles.abstract: Research examining associations between social media usage (SMU) and adolescent psychological wellbeing has relied on cross-sectional self-report data, limiting understanding of specific social media behaviours and within-person variability. To address these limitations, the present study combined an objective experimental task with Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) to investigate associations between adolescents’ SMU styles, momentary affect, and trait depressive symptoms. 229 older adolescents (110 females; Mage = 22.60, 18-25 years old) completed the Social Networking Site Behaviour Task, which classifies SMU along a passive to interactive continuum, across three days (573 datapoints). Trait depressive symptoms were assessed on Day 1 using the Maryland Trait and State Depression Scale, while momentary affect was measured on each day using the International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Linear mixed-effects models revealed between-person variability in SMU style. Positive affect was significantly associated with more interactive SMU (liking and commenting relative to scrolling), whereas negative affect and trait depressive symptoms were not significantly associated with SMU style. Our findings suggest that SMU styles reflect both stable individual differences and dynamic within-person variation associated with positive affective states. This demonstrates the value of combining objective behavioural measures with longitudinal EMA design to advance understanding SMU and psychological wellbeing.

articles.title: Eat your vegetables: Exploring food learning cues in 12-month-old infants
articles.authors: Camille Rioux; Karola Schlegelmilch; Annie E. Wertz
articles.abstract: Food learning in early life largely relies on social learning. Previous research has shown that infants learn something is edible when they directly observe someone else eating it. However, the role of other forms of food-related social information remains largely unknown. Food processing actions (e.g., chopping, mashing) are essential components of human food behaviors and a ubiquitous part of infants’ everyday lives. Here we examined whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to control actions and (ii) learn that novel foods are edible after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them. We tested 12-month-olds’ responses to three different actions: eating, food processing, and a control action (touch). First, we showed infants side-by-side videos of an adult performing two different actions with novel foods across three between-subjects conditions and measured their gaze and pupil dilation with an eye-tracker. Then, we offered infants the novel foods shown in the videos and measured their choices and eating behaviors. Our eye-tracking results indicate that infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to the control action, and show increased pupil dilation for the control action relative to the two actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting). When asked to choose which novel food they could eat, infants chose the novel food they saw an actor eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the control action. These findings help identify important mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

articles.title: Yuck is in the eye of the beholder: Disgust, but not anger, guides 14-month-old infants' person-specific expectations about food preferences
articles.authors: Camille Rioux; Olivier Mascaro
articles.abstract: We investigated whether infants use emotional expressions — a ubiquitous social signal — to learn about food and food preferences. Across two experiments, 14-month-olds completed a combination of Violation-of-Expectancy (VoE) and manual forced-choice tasks. In Experiment 1, an adult reacted to one novel food with disgust and to another neutrally. Subsequently, infants looked significantly longer when she ate the disgusted food than the other one. Thus, infants expected the adult to avoid foods she had found disgusting. This expectation was disgust-specific. When anger replaced disgust in a contrastive condition, infants did not look significantly longer when an adult ate food she had been angry at than food she had reacted neutrally towards.
