The observed advantage does not appear to be explained by a preference for longer responses: Pía produces responses less than half as long as the reference system. Nor by greater scale or general capability, since the reference system surpasses Pía in both. An exploratory analysis by position of the turn within the conversation shows preference indistinguishable from parity in the first third (49.8%) and clearly above it in the middle third (60.6%) and the final third (58.4%), with a significant positive trend (p=0.022); his pattern is compatible with differences between systems becoming more visible when more conversational context is available, without the design being able to identify the responsible mechanism. A second exploratory analysis by risk level A second exploratory analysis by risk level of the conversation shows a
descriptive upward pattern that does not reach statistical significance.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond WEIRD and White: Building a Globally Inclusive Science of Sport Leadership
articles_hidden.authors: Radhika Butalia; Filip Boen; Nicholas de Cruz; S. Alexander Haslam; Rolf van Dick; Katrien Fransen
articles_hidden.abstract: Research in the social sciences overwhelmingly relies on participants drawn from Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies despite the fact that these populations represent about 12% of the world’s population. Moreover, these samples are disproportionately White. Although this limitation has been widely discussed in the social sciences, its implications for sport science remain underexamined. In this expert statement, we use sport leadership research as a test case to illustrate why moving beyond WEIRD and White dominance is critical to building a more inclusive and representative science of sport. First, we discuss how cultural and social contexts shape leadership expectations, perceptions, and effectiveness, thereby calling into question the appropriateness of applying theories developed in WEIRD samples to other contexts. Second, we synthesise the current state of the literature and highlight recent advances, particularly insights from the Cross-Cultural Research on Leadership in Sport (CROLIS) programme. Drawing on these insights, we provide practical and methodological recommendations and identify priorities for future research that together offer a roadmap for building a science of sport leadership in which diverse populations, cultural contexts, and knowledge systems shape equitable knowledge production.

articles_hidden.title: Memories that remain: Image memorability transfers to scene descriptions
articles_hidden.authors: Diana Kollenda; Yee Lee Shing; Katharina Dobs; Benjamin de Haas
articles_hidden.abstract: Some images remain in memory while others fade quickly. Memorability reflects an observer-independent, intrinsic property of an image, which can be predicted by computational models. While semantic content has been proposed as the critical determinant of memorability, it is challenging to disentangle image content from visual features on display. Here, we find that the memorability of scene images transfers to short textual descriptions of those scenes, whether generated by humans or multimodal large language models. Furthermore, new images produced with generative AI from descriptions alone reproduce the memorability of original images. Together, these findings show that semantic content, including interrelations captured in scene descriptions, accounts for a meaningful portion of the variation in scene memorability, and that language serves as an efficient compression of memory-relevant visual content.

articles_hidden.title: Seeking and integrating social information under uncertainty: the role of high stakes and risky others
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline J Charpentier; Xiaodi Hu
articles_hidden.abstract: When making decisions under risk and ambiguity, we often have the opportunity to know what other people did and adjust our decisions. Yet, the cognitive mechanisms underlying how people actively seek social information, and how such information is integrated into choice, remain poorly understood. We addressed this question using a new social risk-ambiguity task in which participants first made baseline decisions under risk and ambiguity, then, in a social block, actively chose whether to view the decisions of two other players before deciding again. Across two large online samples (Ndiscovery=394, Nreplication=378), we found that social information-seeking increased with reward magnitude and reward probability, but was not affected by ambiguity. Individual differences further showed that participants who were more sensitive to reward probability during baseline choice were also more driven by reward probability when seeking information. Social information influenced both risky and ambiguous choices, even though participants weighed their own prior preferences more strongly. Critically, influence was asymmetric: the risky player exerted stronger influence than the safe player, with more risk/ambiguity-averse individuals exhibiting relatively weaker influence from the risky player. Computational modelling revealed a dissociation between two key processes captured by separable parameters: egocentric discounting (weight of individual vs social information) and asymmetry between risky and safe social influence. Together, these findings provide more integrated insights into the cognitive mechanisms underlying baseline choice, social information-seeking, and social influence under uncertainty, as well as the heterogeneity linking them.

articles_hidden.title: The Morality-Effectiveness Disconnect of Pro-environmental Behaviors
articles_hidden.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hege Landsvik
articles_hidden.abstract: Not all pro-environmental behaviors are created equal—some are vastly more effective at mitigating climate change than others. Do people judge the more effective behaviors as proportionally more moral? Five main and six supplemental studies (N = 9,247) across five countries reveal a robust morality-effectiveness disconnect: pro-environmental behaviors that rank better on objective climate-mitigation potential rank worse on individual moral judgments. Laypeople fail to predict this pattern, believing that a positive relationship exists. Further, labeling behaviors by climate impact category reduces the morality-effectiveness disconnect, and detailed impact information reverses it and increases policy endorsement of more effective behaviors over less effective behaviors. While the disconnect primarily stems from effectiveness misperceptions that accurate information can mitigate, we find that personal support for less effective behaviors plays an additional role. Thus, people's moral intuition for climate action appears miscalibrated: moral cognition can undermine the collective welfare that such cognition should presumably promote.

articles_hidden.title: Using the Interpersonal Circumplex in Therapeutic Planning and Intervention for Individuals Experiencing Acculturative Stress
articles_hidden.authors: Serena Z Chen; Aaron L. Pincus
articles_hidden.abstract: We integrate theories and models of acculturative stress and interpersonal behavior to help advance research and practice for clients experiencing acculturative stress. We briefly review Contemporary Integrative Interpersonal Theory (CIIT) and the interpersonal situation framework as an empirically validated heuristic model for case conceptualization and psychotherapy. We then apply CIIT to therapeutic planning and intervention for individuals experiencing acculturative stress, including a clinical example and clinical recommendations.

articles_hidden.title: Social cure goes global: Socioeconomic and cultural factors shape social identifications’ effects on wellbeing across 56 countries.
articles_hidden.authors: Radhika Butalia; Tegan Cruwys; Jolanda Jetten; Catherine Haslam; Katrien Fransen; Stef Van Puyenbroeck; Rolf van Dick; Lies Bongaerts; Filip Boen
articles_hidden.abstract: Social identification has been robustly linked to wellbeing. However, most of this evidence relies on samples from White and WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich,  Democratic) nations. In this study, we tested the association between social identification and wellbeing in a global sample (46,156 participants in 56 countries), and assessed whether socioeconomic and cultural factors could explain variation between countries. Across this sample, social identification was positively associated with wellbeing, but these benefits were not uniform. Identification with family and friends (β = 0.24) showed stronger and more consistent associations with wellbeing than national identification (β = 0.07). While associations between national identification and wellbeing were positive in 93% of countries, they were reliable (i.e., confidence intervals did not cross zero) in fewer than half. The positive association between social identification and wellbeing was stronger in settings characterised by greater wealth and inequality, and varied systematically with cultural values: in less secular and less emancipative societies, national identification was more strongly associated with wellbeing whereas identification with family and friends was less strongly associated with wellbeing. These findings show that promoting wellbeing globally requires attention to the strength and nature of people’s social identifications, and the socioeconomic and cultural conditions in which they are embedded.

articles_hidden.title: Insomnia and Emotion Dysregulation Across the Perinatal Period: Daily and Longitudinal Associations with Anxiety and Depression
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Barrett; Benicio Frey; David L. Streiner; Sheryl Green
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Insomnia is prevalent during pregnancy and the postpartum period and contributes to vulnerability for anxiety and depressive disorders during this time. However, the mechanisms linking sleep disturbance to depressive and anxiety symptoms remain unclear. Emotion dysregulation (ED) and pre-sleep arousal have been proposed as key transdiagnostic processes. This is the first study to integrate daily and longitudinal methods to examine these mechanisms across the perinatal period.
Methods: Data were drawn from a randomized controlled trial evaluating two brief interventions for insomnia during pregnancy and the postpartum. Seventy-five pregnant individuals were assessed across pregnancy and the postpartum using trait measures and 7-day daily surveys at three timepoints. Regression models examined whether prenatal insomnia, ED, and their interaction predicted postpartum depression, anxiety, and worry. Multilevel models tested within-person associations between daily sleep and next-day symptoms, with ED as a moderator, and cluster bootstrap mediation analyses examined pre-sleep arousal as a mediator of sleep–symptom associations.
Results: For postpartum anxiety symptoms, higher prenatal insomnia and ED independently predicted symptoms, with a significant interaction (β = .28, p = .003). For postpartum depressive symptoms, only the insomnia × ED interaction was significant (β = .23, p = .045). For postpartum worry, only baseline worry predicted outcomes. At the within-person level, sleep quality and sleep onset latency predicted next-day anxiety and depression; ED did not moderate these associations. Mediation analyses indicated that daytime anxiety and depressive symptoms predicted poorer sleep quality, sleep onset latency, and sleep efficiency through increased pre-sleep arousal.
Conclusions: Findings support a pathway linking insomnia and ED to perinatal anxiety and depression. Results suggest that prenatal ED is associated with heightened vulnerability to the mental health consequences of insomnia and identify pre-sleep arousal as a key mechanism linking daytime affect to sleep disruption. Clinical implications for perinatal mental health are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Anxious avoidance as disrupted exploration
articles_hidden.authors: Vanessa M Brown; Alexandre Dombrovski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Avoidance is a hallmark of anxiety. Exposure treatments often help overcome
avoidance, yet why avoidance persists without external reinforcement remains unclear.
We propose that one contributing factor is a failure to adaptively use uncertainty when
deciding whether to explore choices with unknown outcomes. Using reinforcement
learning and explore/exploit paradigms, we examined whether anxious individuals
misestimate the value of exploration. We tested this hypothesis against alternatives—
uncertainty intolerance, punishment sensitivity, and stochastic choice—in a task where
optimal behavior required both increasing and decreasing exploration. Consistent with
our hypothesis, people high in anxiety failed to adjust exploration based on uncertainty,
instead either under-exploring or over-exploring. This deficit was distinct from
intolerance of uncertainty and remained after controlling for other internalizing
symptoms. These findings suggest that anxious avoidance may stem from
misestimating uncertainty and the value of exploration, pointing to new treatment targets
focused on improving adaptive use of uncertainty.

articles_hidden.title: A Qualitative Investigation of Emotion Dysregulation in Perinatal Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Emily Barrett; Danielle Rice; Talia Tissera; Benicio Frey; Arela Agako; David L. Streiner; Sheryl Green
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Mood and anxiety disorders are common during the perinatal period, impacting both parental health and infant development. Understanding the core symptoms and processes that underlie these conditions is essential for improving screening and intervention. Emotion dysregulation (ED) is a key transdiagnostic factor, yet research has largely relied on questionnaires and physiological measures of ED that offer limited insight into individuals’ lived experiences. This study aimed to qualitatively explore how individuals with heightened ED understand, experience, and regulate their emotions during pregnancy and the postpartum, and how these experiences differ from pre-pregnancy. Methods: Perinatal participants (N = 16) were recruited within the Women’s Health Concerns Clinic at St. Joseph’s Healthcare, Hamilton. Participants who endorsed experiencing ED were invited to complete a semi-structured qualitative interview related to their experience with ED.  Interview data was analysed using a directed content analysis. Themes: Participants described heightened emotion reactivity during the perinatal period, characterized by rapid mood changes and heightened intensity of anger, shame, guilt, anxiety, sadness, hopelessness, and joy. Participants described feeling unprepared to manage the increased intensity of negative emotions, particularly anger, compounded by reduced access to activities that had previously supported emotion regulation (e.g., self-care or social activities). Factors that contributed to vulnerability included life stressors, sleep disruption, and unmet expectations of both others (e.g., support) and oneself (e.g., coping ability). Conclusions: These findings enrich our understanding of perinatal-specific ED and highlight processes that may inform tailored interventions, that could be preventative in nature, for this vulnerable and understudied population.

articles_hidden.title: Recovery activities and workplace well-being among people with intellectual disabilities: Exploration of the mediating effect of recovery experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Elodie Leclerc; Clément Ginoux; Sandrine Isoard-Gautheur
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Workplace well-being is a key determinant of job retention among people with intellectual disability, a population that faces particularly high levels of labour-market discrimination. Although this group is vulnerable to work-related exhaustion, recovery from work, a process shown to be critical for employee well-being in the general working population, has not yet been examined among these workers. Drawing on recovery theory, the present study explores the role of recovery processes in the workplace well-being of employees with intellectual disability.
Method. A cross-sectional questionnaire assessing leisure activities (i.e., physical, social, creative, mental, virtual, outdoor), off-job recovery experiences (i.e., psychological detachment, relaxation, mastery, control, affiliation, affect) and workplace well-being (i.e., burnout, vigor, need for recovery, job satisfaction) was administered to employees with intellectual disability working in sheltered employment settings in France. Mediation analyses were conducted on 169 valid responses.
Results. Of the six recovery experiences assessed, only affiliation and affect significantly mediated the associations between active leisure activities (physical, social, and outdoor) and workplace well-being.
Conclusion. These findings provide preliminary evidence that relational and affective recovery experiences constitute a pathway through which leisure engagement supports workplace well-being in this population. Given their exploratory nature, they require confirmation in larger, more diverse samples using longitudinal designs.

articles_hidden.title: Idiographic Item Response Theory: Modeling Person-Specific Differential Item Functioning in Intensive Longitudinal Data
articles_hidden.authors: Joshua B Gilbert; Edward J. Kim; Zachary Himmelsbach; Esther Ulitzsch; Lijin Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: Idiographic theories of psychological measurement emphasize that the relationships between item responses and a latent trait may vary across individuals, yet typical item response theory (IRT) models assume item parameters are constant across persons. We propose an IRT approach for modeling person-specific (idiographic) heterogeneity in item functioning in intensive longitudinal data. We extend the two-parameter logistic IRT model to allow item location parameters to vary across individuals through person-by-item interaction random effects. We apply a Bayesian estimator to estimate item-specific interaction variances and use a regularizing spike-and-slab likelihood mixture to identify items with non-negligible heterogeneity. A simulation study indicates that the model recovers such heterogeneity reasonably well when person sample sizes and the number of repeated measurements are at least moderate. We then apply our approach to empirical data from a depression study and find substantial variation across items in the degree of person-specific item functioning. The proposed model and estimator contribute to emerging work on idiographic measurement by extending IRT to settings where repeated observations can be used to estimate individual departures from group-level item parameters, providing a new tool for studying differential item functioning, measurement invariance, and broader forms of individual variation in intensive longitudinal data.

articles_hidden.title: Digital mental health interventions for anxiety: An umbrella review and multiverse meta- analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Constantin Yves Plessen; Olga-Maria Panagiotopoulou; Clara Miguel; Marketa Ciharova; Davide Papola; Darin Pauley; Eirini Karyotaki; Pim Cuijpers
articles_hidden.abstract:
Several meta-analyses and meta-reviews have yielded inconclusive results on the efficacy
of digital mental health interventions for anxiety disorders. To address this discrepancy, we
conducted an umbrella review and multiverse meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials with
no restrictions on intervention type, target group, format, control condition, or diagnosis. Studies
focusing on comorbid anxiety were excluded. We screened 10.942 records and retrieved 1.263
full texts, identifying 10 meta-analyses and 81 randomized controlled trials meeting inclusion
criteria. Unfortunately, the majority of included meta-analyses and primary investigations were
of suboptimal quality, with possible conflicts of interest. Only two meta-analyses provided
suggestive evidence, and the majority yielded weak evidence. Digital interventions demonstrated
stronger evidence for the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder than other anxiety disorders.
The multiverse meta-analysis calculated 2.220 additional meta-analyses, with an average effect
size of Hedges’ g = 0.65 with 79% of the meta-analyses reaching at least a small effect size.
Results suggest the overall robustness of digital interventions, with larger effect sizes observed
for guided interventions, internet-based interventions, and comparisons with waitlist control
groups. Nonetheless, we caution against overinterpreting findings given the overall low quality
of evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Mindscapes of Second Language Acquisition: A New Perspective on the Cognitive Inquiry of Language
articles_hidden.authors: Junya Fukuta
articles_hidden.abstract: This book repositions second language acquisition (SLA) within cognitive science by developing a new epistemological framework for explaining language learning. Grounded in functional realism and contemporary mechanistic explanation, it advances the Causal-Mechanistic Systems Research Programme that retains a commitment to organised cognitive systems while incorporating complexity, embodiment, and sociality. From this perspective, the book reconsiders how L2 knowledge should be conceptualised, how language interacts with other dimensions of cognition, and how linguistic knowledge emerges and develops. Rather than treating descriptive categories, correlations, or task-dependent effects as explanations in themselves, it asks what underlying mechanisms generate the observable phenomena of SLA. By applying this perspective across major theoretical domains of second language research, the book presents SLA as a distinctive empirical arena for investigating the organisation, development, and adaptability of human cognition.

articles_hidden.title: What difference do cash transfers make? Understanding impacts and mechanisms from cash transfer recipients and communities in Malawi and Lesotho.
articles_hidden.authors: Mirela Zaneva; Josphine Hapazari; Theodora Khofi; Christopher James Graham; Eunbi Han; Shruti; Aswathi Surendran; Rizwana Amin; Roseline Dzekem Dine; Hangala Siachiwena
articles_hidden.abstract: Cash transfers are a common poverty alleviation intervention, yet qualitative reports of recipients’ lived experiences are limited. Without these perspectives, policy frameworks risk reducing beneficiaries to passive inputs in programmatic equations. This means potentially overlooking the social meanings, moral negotiations, and relational dynamics through which transfers are actually received, used, perceived, and redistributed. To address this gap, we analyzed 74 in-depth interviews with cash transfer recipients and their household members in rural Malawi and Lesotho. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we created four themes: 1) “With my poverty it can’t work”: Enough to survive, not enough to change, 2) “I can’t be eating in my house while my children are hungry next door”: Grandmothers and the obligation to share, 3) “I am already worried as to what I will be doing”:  Psychological relief and stress intertwine, 4) “Sky-falling” and “satanic” money: Notions of deservingness produce stigma and jealousy. Recipients consistently noted improvement in food security, while effects on mental health and social relationships were more mixed. We argue that recipient-centered reports complement and strengthen quantitative evidence about the impacts and mechanisms of cash transfers. We discuss specific policy recommendations, such as larger and more predictable payments, better communication, and sensitive disbursement options, gender-sensitive support, and more active monitoring of psychosocial and community effects in order to mitigate potential negative impacts. Finally, we argue there is a need for a more ambitious focus on development as the key path to poverty eradication.

articles_hidden.title: Social influence and information cascades in experience-based decisions
articles_hidden.authors: Kiri Kuroda; Simon Kai Ciranka; Dirk U. Wulff; Ralf Kurvers
articles_hidden.abstract: Many consequential decisions are made in environments where outcome probabilities are not explicitly described but must be inferred from experience. In most modern environments, this information search takes place in the presence of others. Yet, the role of social influence in experience-based decisions has been largely overlooked, leaving it unclear how personal and social information combine to shape what people sample, when they stop searching, and what they finally choose. Here, we address all three decision stages. In a preregistered study, participants could freely sample two options before making a final choice, either alone (solo condition) or while observing the final choices of their group members (group condition). We developed a modeling framework and show that social influence left sampling unaffected but altered stopping and choice. Participants searched longer when the group was more divided and stopped earlier when the majority choice agreed with their own personal sampling information. Consequently, they drew fewer samples and encountered fewer rare events than solo participants. When choosing, group members copied others' choices only when their personal information was ambiguous. Comparing decision sequences in groups with a solo baseline, complemented with agent-based simulations, showed that this strategy gave rise to mild information cascades, with decisions in groups being more similar to each other than in a solo baseline. Our results reveal how social influence shapes search, stopping, and choice, and how these individual-level decision rules scale up to collective dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: (Im)moral autobiographical memory: the role of morality in past and future personal events
articles_hidden.authors: Mara Stockner; Jessica Talbot; Gianmarco Convertino; Giuliana Mazzoni
articles_hidden.abstract: Autobiographical memory can be distorted, supporting the maintenance of a positive self-image (e.g., self-enhancement concept. In this line, evidence has shown that memories of immoral actions can be characterized by distortions (e.g., less details or blurry) and elicit a so-called “immoral amnesia” (e.g., Kouchaki & Gino, 2016). In the present study, we aimed at replicating the phenomenological characteristics of ABMs regarding moral and immoral actions participants performed in their past and aimed at verifying, for the first time, if analogous phenomenological characteristics of immoral vs. moral actions can also be found for personal future events. 68 participants recalled subjectively perceived moral and immoral past events, imagined moral and immoral personal future events and evaluated the retrieved events based on a series of phenomenological characteristics. Our results replicate the so-called “immoral amnesia” both for past and future events, showing that immoral (vs. moral) events were objectively and subjectively perceived more distant in time, less vivid, contained subjectively fewer visual and sensorial details, and involved people were less clearly represented. However, our results also show some differences between past and future mental representations: future immoral (vs. moral) events were, for instance, evaluated as less immoral and as less important compared to past immoral events. Overall, our findings suggest that morality moderates aspects of both past and future autobiographical processing, and humans appear to adopt a self-enhancement approach to evaluating their own past and future transgressions.

articles_hidden.title: The Functional Role of Eye Movements in Episodic Remembering Depends on the Individual and the Memory: Evidence Across the Phantasia Spectrum
articles_hidden.authors: Sylvana Brewer; Mikael Johansson; Roger Johansson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Eye movements are thought to support episodic remembering by reinstating aspects of the content and relational structure of previous experiences. However, it remains unclear whether this functional role differs across mental imagery phenotypes spanning the spectrum from aphantasia to hyperphantasia. To address this question, we experimentally manipulated eye movements during retrieval in participants sampled broadly across the imagery spectrum.
Gaze reinstatement occurred reliably during free viewing and predicted recollection. Restricting eye movements significantly impaired recollection, providing experimental evidence that the opportunity to move the eyes contributes functionally to episodic remembering. Critically, the benefit of free viewing depended on imagery ability, showing a nonlinear relationship with imagery vividness that was greatest at intermediate levels and reduced toward both ends of the imagery spectrum. Imagery vividness did not systematically predict gaze reinstatement itself, indicating a distinction between spontaneous oculomotor behaviour and its functional contribution to remembering. This relationship became increasingly pronounced with greater visual exploration during encoding: memories with a more extensive visual sampling history showed greater subsequent dependence on eye movements during retrieval. Spatial imagery provided an additional independent source of variation, with individuals high in spatial imagery exhibiting greater impairment when eye movements were restricted.
These findings demonstrate that the functional role of eye movements in episodic remembering is not uniform across mental imagery phenotypes but depends jointly on imagery ability and the extent of visual exploration during encoding. More broadly, they suggest that eye movements constitute a flexible retrieval mechanism whose contribution varies across individuals and memories.

articles_hidden.title: Social and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Risk and Resilience in Young People: The Longitudinal THRIVE-study
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth E. L. Buimer; Maximilian König; Pauline Wessels; Hannah Dorsman; Antoinette Haverhals; THRIVE consortium; Peter Bos; Geert-Jan Will; Anne-Laura Van Harmelen
articles_hidden.abstract:
More than half of the children and adolescents worldwide experience at least one form of childhood adversity (e.g., abuse, neglect or bullying) whilst growing up. Childhood adversity is among the strongest predictors of mental health problems in adolescence and adulthood. Yet, some individuals show resilient functioning, meaning they have good mental health and well-being despite their exposure to childhood adversity. Childhood adversity is thought to affect mental health through its impact on neurocognitive functioning, for example through blunted social feedback learning and biased emotion and threat processing. The neurocognitive social transactional model suggests that such childhood adversity related neurocognitive functioning may ultimately lead to reductions in the quality and quantity of social relations and increases in stressful experiences with peers over time, increasing the risk for mental health problems. However, empirical evidence to support this theoretical framework is scarce. Therefore, the longitudinal Towards Health and Resilience in Volatile Environments (THRIVE) study is set out to investigate the dynamics of psychological, social, and neurobiological mechanisms underlying mental health functioning in adolescents aged 18-24 years with a history of childhood adversity.

The ongoing THRIVE study aims to recruit 288 participants aged 18-24 years who retrospectively self-report childhood adversity (current N=220). This longitudinal neuroimaging study consists of 6 sessions including an in-unit session, during which participants undergo extensive testing including salivary cortisol measures, emotion labelling measures, as well as functional neuroimaging (whilst completing the Montreal Imaging Stress Task and the Social Feedback Learning Task). In the longitudinal part of the study, participants fill out online questionnaires at 5 time points (i.e. every three months) to map the dynamics and associations of social support, mental health, and stressful events, over time. Using the data collected at the in-unit session, we aim to test whether childhood adversity is associated with biased emotion processing, blunted feedback learning and enhanced stress responses, while social support may moderate these effects (i.e. ‘social stress buffering’). The longitudinal component of the THRIVE study allows us to test our hypothesis that mental health problems arise because childhood adversity shapes neurocognitive functioning in a way that, over time, reduces social support and increases social stress. By unravelling how social functioning contributes to resilient functioning after childhood adversity, the THRIVE study will aid crucial knowledge and ultimately help intervention and prevention efforts.

The THRIVE study has been approved by The Medical Ethics Committee Leiden - The Hague - Delft (NL80017.058.21) on July 5th, 2022  and has been co-created with the Augeo Youth Task Force (a panel of young adults with childhood adversity, https://www.augeo.nl/jongerentaskforce). The Augeo Youth Task Force is involved in every step of the empirical cycle to make sure the perspective and knowledge of young people with childhood adversity are incorporated. The results of the THRIVE study will be disseminated through preprints, peer-reviewed scientific publications, scientific presentations, media and public outreach.

articles_hidden.title: Nothing “Evaluative“ about Evaluative Priming?  Semantic Relatedness Beyond Evaluation Is Not Necessary for a Facilitation of Evaluative Judgements
articles_hidden.authors: Manuel Becker; Marie Jakob; Karl Christoph Klauer
articles_hidden.abstract: Ever since Zajonc proposed that preferences need no inferences, psychologists have debated whether evaluations can be conceptualized and measured independently of co-activated semantic content. One prominent arena for this debate has been the Evaluative Priming Task, which tracks the effects of conflicting or congruent evaluative relationships between stimuli. Surprisingly, two prior lines of research found that effects of evaluative congruency in the task do not emerge in the absence of additional semantic relationships. This not only conflicts with other findings, but also challenges dominant theoretical accounts of the task, whose assumptions entail that congruency effects should arise irrespectively. In Studies 1 and 2 (Ns=81, 85), we re-examine these two lines of research and show that when vulnerabilities in the original experimental and analytical designs are rectified, evaluative congruency effects do reliably occur (even in the absence of strong semantic relationships). A third study (N=80), that implements strong semantic relationships under especially controlled conditions, also yields reliable congruency effects. In Study 4 (N=81), the trials with low semantic relatedness from the first three studies are combined, replicating consistent and reliable, but small congruency effects. Our results thereby strengthen models that accommodate an independent role of evaluations, and we illustrate how these models might be modified to account for an augmenting influence of semantic relatedness. Currently, in domains for which evaluations and their measurement are integral (like the measurement of race-based evaluations, consumer or health behavior), the pronounced and potentially biasing effects of semantic relatedness remain largely unrecognized as a serious confound.

articles_hidden.title: Computational and neural signatures of volatility learning in infancy: Links with temperament and the early caregiving environment
articles_hidden.authors: Dimana V. Atanassova; Nemes Zsuzsanna; Marlene Meyer; Sabine Hunnius
articles_hidden.abstract:
Infants demonstrate a remarkable ability to learn from statistical patterns. Yet, in probabilistic environments, successful learning requires distinguishing random variability from true changes in the underlying contingency (i.e. volatility). However, the extent to which successful volatility learning in infancy is modulated by environmental and temperamental differences is still unclear, as well as the extent to which infant neural processing reflects learning from changes. To answer these questions, we investigated the computational and neural basis of volatility learning in 11-month-old infants and examined how temperament (Infant Behavior Questionnaire-Revised; Very Short Form) and features of the early caregiving environment (Comprehensive Early Childhood Parenting Questionnaire) shape individual differences in this process.
Infants (N=77, Mage=331.13±15.25 days; 32 girls, 45 boys) observed a probabilistic environment in which the most likely location of a target periodically changed. Infants learned these contingencies, as reflected in their anticipatory looking, demonstrating sensitivity to environmental volatility. To characterize the computational processes underlying this learning, we used a Hierarchical Gaussian Filter model, which captures how learners update their beliefs about both the current state of the environment and its volatility. Prediction errors derived from this model, in combination with anticipation accuracy, predicted EEG activity 588–714 ms after feedback across a broad fronto-central region, providing evidence that the cognitive mechanisms captured by the model are represented in the infant brain. 
Additionally, we found that individual differences in volatility learning were primarily captured by model-derived change sensitivity: infants with a stronger change sensitivity detected reversals in the volatile environment better and adapted their behavior more rapidly. Change sensitivity was positively related to IBQ Effortful Control, suggesting infants with stronger regulatory capacities also updated their beliefs about volatility in a more optimal fashion. 
infants with higher Effortful Control detected environmental reversals more rapidly and showed more optimal belief updating. Finally, Positive Discipline was associated with higher Effortful Control, although its indirect association with change sensitivity was not significant. Finally, in a Structural Equation Model, we found that higher Effortful Control was predicted by stronger Positive Discipline, although the indirect pathway to change sensitivity was not significant. 
Together, these findings identify early computational and neural signatures of hierarchical volatility learning and highlight emerging temperament and caregiving influences on adaptive learning in infancy.

articles_hidden.title: A low-dimensional hypothesis for cognition and the human brain
articles_hidden.authors: Leonardo Bonneti; Barbara A. P. Grosjean; Chiara Malvaso; Nikita Kudriavtsev; Gemma Fernandez-Rubio; Mattia Rosso
articles_hidden.abstract: The human brain is among the most complex biological systems known, yet a growing body of evidence suggests that its activity consistently exhibits low-dimensional organisation. Across behavioural states, recording modalities, spatial scales, and analytical approaches, large-scale neural dynamics can often be described by a surprisingly limited number of latent processes expressed through coordinated large-scale spatiotemporal patterns. This observation presents a fundamental paradox: how can a system capable of remarkably flexible cognition operate within such constrained dynamical structure? Here, we propose a low-dimensional hypothesis for cognition. We argue that cognition depends on the emergence of low-dimensional latent processes from complex neural activity, their reconfiguration according to internal and external demands, and the interactions among them. Within this framework, cognition arises not from unconstrained high-dimensional neural activity, but from the efficient organisation of neural dynamics into latent processes and their interactions. We review converging evidence for low-dimensional organisation across brain activity and cognition and outline a set of falsifiable predictions concerning cognitive demands, learning, development, aging, neurological and psychiatric disorders, pharmacological interventions, and social interaction. Finally, we consider whether this principle extends across spatial scales and whether analogous organisation emerges in artificial neural networks. Altogether, we propose low-dimensional organisation as a candidate principle for understanding the neural substrate of cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Contextual modulation of fear extinction as predictor of exposure therapy effectiveness
articles_hidden.authors: Lotte Stemerding; Mirjam Kampman; Agnes van Minnen; Gert-Jan Hendriks; Vanessa Anna van Ast; Rianne de Kleine
articles_hidden.abstract: Exposure therapy is an effective treatment for disorders characterized by fear and anxiety, but not all patients achieve symptom relief and many relapse outside of the original therapeutic context. Alterations in fear extinction – widely considered the central mechanism of exposure therapy – are observed in clinical populations, and have been linked to exposure treatment outcomes. However, extinction learning deficits alone cannot explain why fear returns when contextual conditions change. It is therefore pivotal to investigate the predictive value of contextual modulation of extinction learning for long-term exposure success. In this study, we examined whether contextual modulation of fear and safety learning in a Pavlovian fear-conditioning paradigm predicted intensive exposure treatment outcomes in patients with PTSD, OCD, and panic disorder (n = 109). We hypothesised that better contextual modulation would predict more favourable treatment outcomes across patient groups. Before treatment, participants completed fear acquisition and extinction in two different contexts, and three test phases assessing conditioned responses in the extinction and acquisition context, and a novel context. Fear responses were indexed by US expectancies and distress ratings. Symptom improvements were assessed using disorder-specific clinician-rated and self-report measures, as well as a transdiagnostic index of symptom distress. Our findings show that greater extinction context retention predicted more symptom reduction post-treatment, although effects were not consistent across outcome measures. These findings offer new insights into mechanisms that may underlie exposure success and highlight the translational value of contextual retention of extinction learning in fear-conditioning paradigms.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Validation of Home Factors for Critical Reading Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Jenni Ruotsalainen; Leena Paakkari; Mari Manu; Emmi Ulvinen; Jenni Salminen; Kamil Kuracki; Minna Palmu; Minna Torppa
articles_hidden.abstract: Today, children need critical reading skills from an early age, making it essential to explore how these skills can be supported in the home environment. Since no measure currently exists for examining home factors that may affect critical reading development, this study aimed to develop and validate scale for families with children aged 7–16 years. The study included three phases in Finland: 1) item generation, 2) item selection through two pilot studies (n=260; n=280), and 3) validation of the scale with two separate datasets from Finland (n=11,090; n=328). External validity was examined in a Polish sample (n=120). Initially, 178 items were generated, 82 of which were selected for piloting. Through the pilot studies, the 14 best-performing items were selected for validation. A six-factor structure was identified for the scale, referred to as the Home Factors for Critical Reading (home-CR) scale: 1) Critical reading practices, 2) Attention to child initiatives, 3) Control of media use, 4) Reading interest and expectations, 5) Valuing knowledge, and 6) Rigid thinking patterns. The consistency of the factor structure across samples and its alignment with theoretical constructs supported the construct validity of the scale. Criterion validity was examined in relation to the number of books at home, parental reading frequency, and digital parenting, and the home-CR scale was found to be related to—yet distinct from—these constructs. The confirmatory factor analysis loading structure and test–retest results supported the reliability of the scale. The iterative, validity-driven development process yielded a brief, multidimensional home-CR scale.

articles_hidden.title: Directional Asymmetry in Reasoning About National and Religious Identity Is Category-Specific: Evidence From Palestine, Israel, and the United States
articles_hidden.authors: Mostafa Salari Rad; Jeremy Ginges
articles_hidden.abstract: Judgments about whether a person can gain or lose a group identity may depend both on which category is at stake and on the direction of transfer. For national identity, people judge that an outgroup-born child raised by the ingroup becomes one of us more readily than an ingroup-born child raised by the outgroup becomes one of them (Rad & Ginges, 2018). That work varied which outgroup was named but never which category, leaving open whether the asymmetry is a general property of reasoning about ingroups, is specific to nationality, or varies with how membership in a category is represented, which differs across populations. We tested these alternatives in settings where religion and nationality pick out nearly the same adversary, using switched-at-birth tasks with Muslim-Palestinians (N = 1,205), Americans (N = 989), and religious Israeli Jews (N = 280). The asymmetry appeared for national identity in all three samples and did not depend on the outgroup being the adversary. For religious identity it was absent among Palestinians and Americans, but present among Israeli Jews and not reliably different from nationality's. Across conditions and studies, directional asymmetry appeared only where membership was treated as substantially fixed at birth, and where it appeared it was carried almost entirely by judgments of what ingroup upbringing confers rather than of what birth transmits. The asymmetry is therefore neither a general feature of group boundaries nor a property of nationality in particular, but emerges where membership is understood as substantially fixed at birth.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring the effective polarity and level along the excitation patterns produced by focussed cochlear-implant stimulation
articles_hidden.authors: Robert P. Carlyon; Francois Guerit; John M. Deeks
articles_hidden.abstract:
Three experiments estimated the effective polarity and level of neural activation
produced by trains of “baseline” symmetric biphasic pulses, where the order of the phases
of each pulse was anodic-cathodic (AC) or cathodic-anodic (CA). Detection thresholds were
measured for trains of quadrupolar-mode anodic-leading pseudomonophasic probe pulses,
where each pulse was presented immediately after a baseline pulse or in quiet. Thresholds
were substantially lower in the presence than in the absence of the baseline in several
conditions, including for monopolar baselines in CA order. This unmasking was also
observed with wide-bipolar (BP+10) and wide-tripolar (TP=3, TP+5) baselines, whenever
the probe was presented to an electrode where the second phases of the baseline pulses
were anodic. Because the polarity of the baseline varied across the electrode array for BP
and TP stimuli, this allowed us to measure reversals in the effective polarity of the
baseline stimulus along its excitation pattern. The unmasking is attributed to constructive
charge interactions between the first (anodic) phase of each probe pulse with the second
phase of the preceding baseline pulse. The results are compared to voltage profiles for
each baseline measured along the electrode array, and are discussed in terms of potential
implications for the development of improved cochlear-implant stimulation methods.

articles_hidden.title: Prospective associations between depressive symptoms and cognitive function remain uncertain: A reanalysis of Wang et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Wang et al. reported longitudinal findings that were interpreted as evidence that depressive symptoms contribute to subsequent deterioration in cognitive function. However, statistically significant cross-lagged coefficients are not, by themselves, sufficient evidence for a genuine prospective effect because similar estimates can arise through alternative statistical processes. Using simulated data constructed to reproduce the sample size and correlation structure reported by Wang et al., we assessed the stability of the reported conclusions across several defensible analytical specifications. Results differed markedly depending on the model employed. Some specifications suggested positive prospective associations, whereas others indicated negative or statistically non-significant relationships. When estimates from all specifications were synthesized using meta-analytic procedures, no significant overall effects emerged. These findings indicate that the evidence presented by Wang et al. does not provide a stable foundation for concluding that depressive symptoms prospectively influence cognitive function. Consistent with recommendations from the multiverse-analysis literature, conclusions should be based on evidence aggregated across reasonable analytical alternatives rather than on the results of a single model.

articles_hidden.title: Apparent kindling in a washboard potential model of mood dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Jihwan Myung
articles_hidden.abstract: The kindling hypothesis proposes that repeated stressors or mood episodes leave persistent sensitizing traces that lower the threshold for subsequent episodes. Evidence in bipolar disorder is mixed, and recurrence alone does not establish such persistent change. Here I propose a phenomenological landscape in which progression can appear causally linked without being so. Mood state moves on a multi-well washboard potential landscape. Kindling would persistently change the geometry of the landscape, and circadian and sleep-related inputs reversibly tilt it. In an illustrative four-well landscape, two inner wells represent normal daily mood variation, while two outer wells represent depression-like and mania-like states. The circadian phase then changes the accessibility of existing states without altering the landscape itself. This distinction provides a complementary account of two clinical observations: the diurnal direction of mood switches reported in rapid-cycling bipolar disorder, and the rapid but transient remission of depression during wake therapy. Circadian organization should add predictive information beyond episode history, and the tilted washboard model suggests chronotherapeutic interventions timed to internal circadian phase.

articles_hidden.title: From Womb to Brain: A Systematic Review of the Impact of Prenatal Maternal Anxiety on Paediatric Brain Structure and Function
articles_hidden.authors: Noa Lily Anthony; Jonathan Ipser; Sheri-Michelle Koopowitz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Prenatal maternal anxiety has been implicated in altered paediatric brain structure and function, but findings from neuroimaging studies are heterogeneous. A PRISMA-aligned systematic review was conducted to evaluate associations between prenatal maternal anxiety and paediatric brain structure and function. A secondary aim was to identify potential sensitive periods across gestation.
Methods: Electronic databases were searched for studies examining associations between prenatal anxiety and paediatric brain structure and function. Eligible papers used magnetic resonance imaging in children exposed to prenatal anxiety. Of 2,668 records retrieved, 1,701 unique records remained after deduplication and 12 met inclusion criteria. These studies included 1082 mother-child dyads with neuroimaging data. Maternal ages ranged from 18 to 45 years and paediatric imaging ages spanned from 5 days to 7 years of age.
Results: Ten of the 12 studies reported statistically significant associations between prenatal maternal anxiety and paediatric neuroimaging outcomes. Associations of mixed directionality were reported across structural, diffusion and functional modalities, involving fronto-limbic regions (including the amygdala and hippocampus), their connecting white-matter pathways (including the uncinate fasciculus, cingulum and fornix), and amygdala-centred functional networks. Trimester-specific findings indicated that anxiety measured during mid- to late gestation was consistently associated with variation in infant limbic development.
Conclusions: This review suggests that prenatal maternal anxiety is associated with variation in paediatric fronto-limbic development. Although the evidence does not establish causality or intervention effectiveness, the findings support the importance of recognising and addressing prenatal maternal anxiety as part of broader maternal and child health initiatives and highlight the need for longitudinal studies to identify mechanisms and intervention targets.

articles_hidden.title: Interactions between working memory and attention depend on remembered feature dimension
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Thayer; Thomas C Sprague
articles_hidden.abstract: Prominent theories of visual search state that goal-relevant information is maintained in working memory (WM) to guide attention to relevant, searched-for items. Prioritization from WM is sufficiently strong to direct attention towards items that are irrelevant to current search goals. These ‘incidental capture’ results have typically been observed when remembering color or shape stimuli, but, in principle, should similarly occur using other strong guiding features such as motion. However, recent work suggests that neural representations of remembered motion directions are transformed into spatial coordinates. If so, then remembered stimuli which can easily be spatially recoded (e.g., remembered motion direction) should not interfere with visual search when feature-matching distractors are present any more than interference caused by a salient distractor that does not match the contents of WM. We replicated the traditional incidental capture finding for color: distractors matching the remembered color captured attention more than feature singletons. In contrast, when participants were required to remember a motion direction, capture was equal across distractor conditions: salient distractors captured attention, but no additional capture was observed when the remembered motion direction matched the distracting motion direction. Intriguingly, responses were faster when the search target was at a location that neural studies predict would be prioritized if remembered motion was spatially recoded. Our results indicate that some features in WM are more likely to impact attentional processing than others and that this difference in attentional capture between feature dimensions may emerge due to the ability to reformat memory representations.

articles_hidden.title: Adults’ Experiences of Mathematical Learning Difficulties and Anxiety: Links to Math Self-efficacy, Self-concept, and Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Anni Savikuja; Riikka Sirkko; Pinja Tähti; Riikka Mononen
articles_hidden.abstract: Mathematical skills are valued and required in a rapidly technologically advancing society. At the same time, many adults struggle with their mathematical skills and experience math anxiety. This qualitative study focuses on examining how adults' mathematical learning difficulties and math anxiety have affected their self-concept, self-efficacy, and learning in mathematics. Nine female adults were interviewed, and reflexive thematic analysis was performed on the data. Three main themes were found that described how mathematical learning difficulties and math anxiety are linked to math self-efficacy, self-concept, and learning: 1) self-doubt in mathematics, 2) lack of support in learning mathematics, and 3) avoidance of mathematics. Implications of math teacher education and adults' basic math skill training are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Idiosyncratic Event Segmentation as a Neural Marker of Loneliness
articles_hidden.authors: Chang Lu; Clara Sava-Segal; Elisa C Baek
articles_hidden.abstract: Loneliness negatively affects both mental and physical health, yet the cognitive mechanisms that give rise to feelings of social disconnection remain poorly understood. A hallmark of loneliness is the feeling of being “out of sync” with others. What contributes to these feelings of misalignment with others? Using functional MRI data from two independent datasets (N = 65 and N = 43), in which participants watched naturalistic videos while their brain activity was recorded, we tested whether lonely individuals display atypical event segmentation patterns—a core component of human perception that shapes how people structure, remember, and understand continuous experiences. Using a Hidden Markov Model–based approach, we found that while non-lonely individuals exhibited similarity, lonely individuals’ neural event segmentation patterns were dissimilar to others, particularly in high-order brain regions (e.g., the default mode network). Furthermore, we found that loneliness was also linked to greater deviations from the group’s normative neural segmentation patterns in certain videos, as indicated by poorer model fit to the group’s average model. These findings suggest that loneliness is linked to unique neural organizations of continuous experiences, revealing a potential cognitive mechanism through which loneliness is characterized by divergent structuring of experience.

articles_hidden.title: Load-Dependent Parameter Scaling in Visual Working Memory Models Reveals the Role of Decoding in Retrieval
articles_hidden.authors: Hang Qian; Paul Michael Garrett; Yi Liu; Philip L. Smith
articles_hidden.abstract: We examined how recent models of continuous visual working memory (VWM) retrieval express capacity limitations through fitted parameters, and whether these expressions follow the inverse square-root scaling predicted by the sample-size model. Through simulations, we generated response errors from a Poisson population-coding model in which increased memory load was implemented as reduced neural population size per item. We then fitted three continuous VWM models that differed in their noise assumptions and decision rules, comparing model-variants in which load affected either representational dispersion or signal amplitude. The parameter that captured capacity-related change depended systematically on the decoder used to transform population activity into a response estimate. Under maximum-likelihood decoding, reduced population size was expressed primarily through changes in dispersion. Under maximum-output decoding, the same manipulation was expressed primarily through changes in amplitude. We then applied the same model-comparison logic to empirical data from a post-cue continuous memory-reproduction task, in which participants reported either color or orientation of a stimulus after encoding both features. Although the two feature domains produced markedly different error distributions, they both favored scaling of the amplitude parameter with set size. These findings show that parameters in continuous VWM models do not merely summarize response-error distributions; they also reflect assumptions about how population-level representations are decoded into behavior. Set-size related parameter changes should therefore be interpreted with consideration of the assumed decoding process, rather than as decoder-independent measures of memory precision or signal strength.

articles_hidden.title: Behaviour Change Strategies for Reducing Meat Consumption: A Multi-Level Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah A. E. Chamberlain; Andreas K Jaeger; Xiaoxiao Chen; Don Hine
articles_hidden.abstract: Dietary change can help to reduce the food-sector contributions to climate change, with reduced meat consumption being an environmentally impactful behaviour that can be promoted using behavioural interventions. While research supports that interventions can reduce meat consumption, substantial variation in outcomes has limited our understanding of which intervention approaches are most effective and how their effects relate to the behavioural determinants they are designed to influence. With previous reviews generally being restricted to specific intervention approaches, settings, or types of outcome assessment, it remains unclear for whom and under what conditions interventions are most effective. This multi-level meta-analysis sought to address this gap through synthesising a broad range of meat reduction interventions (66 studies, 121 effect sizes, 72,832 participants), which were classified using a determinant-based integrative framework. Moderator analyses were used to identify influential intervention, participant, and methodological characteristics. Overall, interventions were found to have a small-to-moderate effect on reducing meat intake (Hedges’ g =  -0.39, 95% CI [-0.50, -0.28]). Intervention approach was a significant moderator, with combination approaches followed by choice architecture having the strongest effects on reducing consumption. Gender significantly moderated intervention effectiveness, with interventions being less effective when samples contained a higher proportion of men. Outcome measure also significantly moderated intervention effectiveness, with larger effects observed for objective measures than subjective or hypothetical assessments. These findings suggest that combining intervention approaches to address multiple behavioural determinants may be particularly effective for promoting environmentally impactful dietary behaviour change, while highlighting the need for interventions targeting male populations.

articles.title: Fossil-Fuel Plant Retirement Disputes and Grid Reliability During the Energy Transition
articles.authors: Peter C. Baker
articles.abstract: Recent fossil-fuel plant retirement disputes show how difficult it can be to maintain grid reliability while the energy grid is undergoing so many changes. This paper focuses on two plant retirement disputes, the Eddystone/PJM and J.H. Campbell/MISO cases, and analyzes the policies associated with maintaining grid reliability during the energy transition.  Throughout the analysis, it becomes evident that there is more to the conflict than a simple tradeoff between reliability and decarbonization.  There is a coordination problem between many governing organizations. Plant owners, state regulators, regional grid operators, FERC, NERC, and DOE all have different responsibilities, and their decisions do not always line up. A plant owner may decide that a facility is no longer economical while another institution later argues that it is still needed for reliability. Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act gives DOE the authority to prevent plant closures that are deemed necessary for reliability, regardless of the economics involving the plant.  However, this paper argues that authority should remain a temporary response to a specific reliability problem. If DOE keeps a plant operating, it should be able to show why that plant is needed, who will pay for it, and what has to happen before it can finally retire. The Eddystone and Campbell cases suggest that repeated emergency orders are not just a reliability issue. They are also evidence that retirement decisions and replacement resources are not being coordinated well enough.

articles.title: Single Religious Belonging in Taiwan
articles.authors: Ruiqian Li
articles.abstract: Single religious belonging (SRB), East Asia's standard survey measure of religion, was built for institutional membership, yet religiosity there is additive and hybrid. Critics expect it to fail, leaving every comparison built on it arbitrary. In eight Taiwan Social Change Survey samples and a Pew survey it does not fail: institutional categories hold within a point, and in the 2023 religion module it predicts 25 of 27 religiosity outcomes. Additive religious habitus explains why: SRB measures two things. For Christianity and Yiguandao it measures membership. For Buddhism, Daoism, and folk religion it measures which religious repertoire a person trusts most among those built around the same gods, a primary repertoire as stable as a membership. It moves only around folk religion, which has no fixed label, shifting with its wording and pulling the nones, Buddhism, and Daoism with it. The fix is practice follow-ups and asking what the label means.

articles.title: Os três corpos de uma eleição: Eleitorado, candidaturas e eleitos no Brasil (1998–2026)
articles.authors: Vitor de Moraes Peixoto
articles.abstract:
O eleitorado brasileiro feminizou-se, envelheceu e escolarizou-se em duas décadas. Este artigo
pergunta o que aconteceu com os outros dois corpos de uma eleição, o de quem se apresenta e o de
quem é escolhido, medindo duas distâncias, a das candidaturas até a população e a dos eleitos até as
candidaturas, em cinco dimensões sociográficas e uma sexta, de trajetória política, nas quinze eleições
de 1998 a 2026, sobre o universo de 3,2 milhões de registros do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral. Toda
série é calculada dentro de um de seis grupos de cargos, e não por tipo de eleição, porque cada tipo é
dominado por um cargo só. O resultado central é que as duas distâncias não se movem no mesmo
sentido: no gênero, nos seis grupos de cargos sem exceção, a distância até o eleitorado encolheu e o
filtro da urna cresceu, e nos três grupos de eleição proporcional, que reúnem mais de nove em cada
dez candidaturas do país, a urna absorveu entre metade e três quartos do que o registro fechou. Na
escolaridade e na classe ocupacional a distância persiste, disfarçada pelo crescimento do denominador
populacional; na cor, nenhuma das duas se move. A dimensão que mais separa registro de mandato
é a trajetória política: metade dos assentos legislativos vai a quem tenta a reeleição, e a fração de
estreantes cai ao mínimo da série em 2026.

articles.title: Violence and International Migration in Illiberal Times: The Case of El Salvador’s Authoritarian Transformation
articles.authors: Jeffrey Swindle; Matthew Blanton
articles.abstract: Across a new transnational wave of illiberal governance, tough-on-crime approaches to public safety and migration are growing. The case of El Salvador, in which President Nayib Bukele suspended due process protections and imprisoned suspected gang members in mass beginning in late March 2022 under a State of Exception policy, offers a window into this process. Turning to a combination of administrative datasets and cross-national surveys, we show that despite tremendous public approval for President Bukele’s strategies as the solution to a long history of persistent gang violence and international migration, violence largely reduced before he implemented the State of Exception, and Salvadorans’ migration intentions have not declined. Moreover, we find no evidence that the policy or Bukele taking office produced a particular reduction in Salvadoran migration to either the U.S. or Mexico compared to Guatemalan and Honduran migration. Nor do we uncover clear evidence that return migration to El Salvador uniquely increased, undercutting conclusions that illiberal tough-on-crime policies like El Salvador’s are likely to address “root causes” of international migration.

articles.title: The Accountability Gap in Sub-Sovereign ESG Finance: A Case Study of Police Administration Oversight in Chiba Prefecture, Japan
articles.authors: Takashi Miyazawa
articles.abstract: This paper examines a critical vulnerability in the methodology of sub-sovereign ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) ratings, utilizing Chiba Prefecture, Japan, as a primary case study. While global ESG frameworks increasingly evaluate local government bonds, rating agencies predominantly rely on macro-level socioeconomic indicators and overarching policy frameworks, creating a significant "measurement gap." We demonstrate how this macro-dependence obscures micro-level governance failures—specifically, the indefinite suspension of complaint processing and the systemic non-creation of official records within police administration. By applying an axiomatic approach grounded in administrative law and corporate governance principles, this study empirically documents the existence of a structural "Accountability Gap" at the operational entry point. The findings highlight the critical need for institutional investors and ESG rating agencies to discount the reliability of sub-sovereign sustainability representations when auditable management evidence is structurally absent.

articles.title: Segregation, Political Economy, and The Longevity of Black and White Americans
articles.authors: Thelonious Lyle Goerz
articles.abstract:
Racial segregation is widely understood to advantage White Americans at the expense of Black
Americans through stratified neighborhoods. However, this overlooks how segregation reshapes the
provision of public goods and fiscal capacity of entire places that affect residents beyond neighborhoods. This paper links 1905–1920 birth cohorts in the 1940 full-count Census to Social Security
death records (N = 2.4 million) and uses multiple instruments and a sibling fixed effects identification strategy to estimate the effect of segregation on the longevity of Black and White Americans.
Results reveal that a 10-point increase in segregation reduces both Black and White longevity by
0.57 and 0.44 years, respectively. I show that tax revenue and welfare spending act as primary
mechanisms for explaining these effects for Blacks and modestly for Whites. These results emphasize the political and policy consequences of segregation that extend beyond neighborhoods and
challenge expectations that Whites materially benefit from segregation.

articles.title: The Non-Binarity of Artificial Intelligence Global Competition: 2018-2025
articles.authors: Wiebke Dorfs; Maximilian Hampel; Joanna J. Bryson
articles.abstract: Technological progress plays a crucial role in international relations. In particular, innovation has long been theorized as instrumental to power transitions. It is therefore unsurprising that the return of China as a global superpower and its technological advances has triggered considerable discussion.  One narrative that has emerged is that of a binary "AI Cold War" competition between China and the US, similar to the 1947-1991 competition between nuclear superpowers. Another though is that the digital and information revolutions should facilitate technology and therefore power diffusion. Here we examine the claim of a binary competition, examining the state and trajectory of global AI competition for the years 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. We use AI patents defended globally in the WIPO database and the market capitalization of the companies holding them as proxies for innovation and market power. We find that the binary narrative underestimates the strength of other actors globally, notably but not exclusively the European Union and Japan. These are comparable to China, and on the innovation metric with the US. In terms of market power, the US is a significant outlier, with an order of magnitude more capital concentration. Our research therefore indicates that any binary AI cold war narrative is not data-led.

articles.title: Early-Career Research Funding Predicts Success in Scientific Careers: A Mathematical Model and Empirical Analysis of Matthew Effects
articles.authors: Yuhei Yamaguchi
articles.abstract: Success breeds success. This simple idea—the Matthew effect, or cumulative advantage—is a classical theme in the science of science. Does obtaining a research grant very early in a researcher’s career, at the very beginning of their academic trajectory, create a performance gap that continues to widen for decades? We approach this question from two sides. First, we build a mathematical model in which talent, publications, research funding, and promotion mutually reinforce one another, and show that even when talent is held constant, the gap in research output between early grant recipients and non-recipients widens over time. We distil this prediction into two hypotheses. Second, we test these hypotheses using a large panel dataset of approximately 40,000 researchers spanning eight broad fields of Japanese academia, drawn from the researchmap database. Using the graduate school of origin as a proxy for talent and prestige, we find that the advantage associated with receiving an early-career fellowship remains positive, statistically significant, and steadily increases over time even after accounting for differences in the institution of origin. In short, even a head start lasting only a few years leaves a lasting mark on a researcher’s career, with its effects continuing to grow more than a decade later. By combining an explicit model of cumulative advantage with large-scale empirical evidence across fields, we quantify how the earliest allocation of research resources shapes the long-term stratification of science.

articles.title: Watching the walls go up: r/wallstreetbets segregated after the GameStop squeeze
articles.authors: Kevin Andrej Quiring
articles.abstract: Online communities keep ideas apart. Across Hacker News and Reddit, concept pairs that should co-occur but never have stay apart at rates far below chance. We call this a wall. The exception was r/wallstreetbets: at chance before 2020, walled by 2024 like everywhere else. Here we report a registered study of when that happened, using rolling quarterly windows over a fresh single-source corpus of 98.1 million Reddit posts and comments, 2019 to 2024. Three predictions committed in advance all pass. The community moves from chance-level mixing to persistent walls, onset 2021-04-01, with zero reversions. In the two windows straddling the January 2021 GameStop episode, suppressed ticker pairs co-mention 28.6 and 30.9 standard deviations above chance. It is the only above-chance excursion this research program has observed, and shuffled data never produce it. Analysis-oriented control communities stay walled through the squeeze, so the excursion is specific to r/wallstreetbets. Two causes were in play, thirty-fold growth during the squeeze and a moderation overhaul after it, and we decided in advance that a mid-2021 onset could point to either. Segregation transitions in online communities can be measured and dated, but their timing alone cannot identify the mechanisms behind them.

articles.title: Ideas that never meet online mark divided communities, not future discoveries
articles.authors: Kevin Andrej Quiring
articles.abstract: In science, two well-studied ideas never discussed together make a likely candidate for a future discovery. Predicting which pair connects next is the aim of literature-based discovery. Whether this holds in online discussion is untested. Here we test it on 200 thousand Hacker News discussions from 2015 to 2017, with a pre-registered replication on 41.5 million Reddit finance posts, 2017 to 2024, using stock tickers. Four pre-registered evaluations use threads, then authors, as documents. Pairs never discussed together, called suppressed pairs, connect no more than popularity and overlapping topics predict. On the Science4Cast benchmark of AI papers, where the effect is known, the same method finds it. The standard test against chance flags connections too easily when document sizes vary. It reported 19 to 24 percent of pairs connecting within authors' quarterly output, yet shuffled data connected more pairs than real data. A per-pair permutation test leaves new connections no higher than false positives produce. Suppressed pairs appear together far below chance: nearly 9 standard deviations at author level, over 100 at thread level. Both results replicate across the 2020-2021 market regime change. Ideas that never meet online mark communities that stay apart, not future discoveries waiting to happen.

articles.title: Value Orientations Emerging from Medical Isolation Following a Life-Threatening Illness: A Phenomenological Study
articles.authors: Great I Am W. Carranza Gismundo; Krisha Mae M. Quinto
articles.abstract: Serious illness and medical isolation can disrupt individuals’ relationships, responsibilities, routines, and expectations for the future, bringing particular priorities and sources of meaning into greater awareness. This study explored the value orientations reflected in the recurring thoughts, concerns, and anticipated situations of individuals who experienced medical isolation following a life-threatening illness. A descriptive phenomenological approach within an interpretivist paradigm was employed. Criterion purposive sampling was used to recruit 13 Filipino adults who had recovered from COVID-19 and experienced medical isolation. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted through phone calls or Facebook Messenger and documented through written interview records. Data collection and analysis proceeded concurrently, with data adequacy guided by inductive thematic saturation. The primary researcher independently analyzed the interview records using Colaizzi’s phenomenological method, while credibility was supported through member checking and independent review of the emergent themes by an experienced hospital-based social worker and a social work educator. Five major themes emerged: Relational Embeddedness and Social Vulnerability; Economic and Occupational Precarity; Meaning-Making, Learning, and Future Orientation; Experiential Reframing and Emotional Restoration; and Transcendence Beyond the Self. The findings indicate that medical isolation was experienced not only as a disruption to physical health but also as a period in which relationships, responsibilities, occupational and economic roles, future aspirations, everyday experiences, spirituality, and concerns for others became particularly salient. Rather than demonstrating permanent value transformation, the findings show how serious illness and enforced isolation can bring existing priorities and sources of meaning into greater awareness. The study highlights the importance of attending to the relational, occupational, economic, existential, and everyday dimensions of illness in health and helping practice.

articles.title: Mental Representations Beyond Survey Responses: Evidence from Gendered Wording
articles.authors: Nora Müller; Lynn-Malou Lutz; Oshrat Hochman; Lisa Hummel Jäckel
articles.abstract:
This study examines the effects of different gender formulations on respondents mental representations of the
people referred to in survey questions, responses to survey questions, and conventional indicators of questionnaire quality.
Using data from a cognitive pretest (N = 466), we compare the generic masculine that is, the use of masculine role nouns to
refer to people regardless of gender, which remains common in German surveys with a gender-inclusive formulation using the
