gender colon and a gender-inclusive neutral formulation. The results show that the linguistic formulation used in survey items
significantly affects respondents mental representations of the people referred to in the survey questions. Compared with both
gender-inclusive formulations, the generic masculine leads to a substantially lower likelihood that respondents include women
in their mental representations. Although wording substantially affected respondents mental representations, responses
differed modestly but significantly across wording conditions only for the politician competence item, whereas responses to
the income question remained stable across wording conditions. Likewise, neither perceived readability nor response times
differed systematically between wording conditions. These findings suggest that relying solely on conventional indicators of
survey quality may overlook meaningful differences in the reference groups respondents have in mind when answering survey
questions, even when observable survey responses remain largely unchanged. Overall, the findings demonstrate the value of
considering respondents’ mental representations alongside conventional indicators of questionnaire quality when evaluating
alternative questionnaire formulations, as conventional survey outcomes alone may overlook meaningful cognitive differences
between wording conditions.

articles.title: Republican, Cosmopolitan, Collective, Threshold: The Political Formations of European Port Cities and Their Democratic Fate
articles.authors: Mudassar Munir
articles.abstract: Port cities across Europe are changing. The docks have been automated, fishing industries have contracted, and the working communities that once organised political and social life around maritime labour have been substantially transformed. This paper asks what these changes mean for the political and social formations that European port cities historically produced. Existing scholarship has established that European port cities constitute a distinctive urban formation, one that developed specific political and social characteristics through centuries of maritime life. The paper examines four recurring political and social formations associated with European port cities: a republican disposition, cosmopolitan pragmatism, collective risk culture, and threshold consciousness. It asks whether these formations are disappearing, taking new institutional forms, or being reworked in ways that preserve their language while changing their democratic substance. The paper focuses on European port cities within the Atlantic, North Sea, and Mediterranean maritime traditions. What is happening to these formations matters not only as a question of urban history, but also as a question of democratic life in contemporary European cities.

articles.title: It's her! Investigating relationship development with social AI chatbots
articles.authors: Nadja Rupprechter; Tobias Dienlin
articles.abstract:
As AI chatbots become integrated into various aspects of everyday life, users increasingly
form parasocial relationships with their digital companions. To understand how such relationships
emerge, we examined how perceived human-likeness fosters parasocial attachment to AI
chatbots. We test a relationship process model in which human-likeness—conceptualized as a
meta-factor comprising anthropomorphism, authenticity, and social presence—promotes
parasocial attachment via user gratifications and interaction behavior. In a preregistered survey of
598 chatbot users from 64 countries, structural equation modeling showed that perceived humanlikeness
was a strong predictor of parasocial attachment. As predicted, this effect was partially
mediated by increased gratifications and interaction. Additional qualitative responses illustrated
how chatbots provide emotional support, role-play, and productivity benefits, alongside concerns
about dependence, social withdrawal, inappropriate behavior, and privacy. Together, the findings
identify human-likeness, gratifications, and interaction as central drivers of parasocial attachment
to AI chatbots.

articles.title: High Agreement, Different Stories: How LLM Classifiers Reshape Demographic Patterns in Survey Data
articles.authors: Chris Soria
articles.abstract: What we learn from open-ended survey data depends on who—or what—does the coding. Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to democratize qualitative analysis, but do high agreement rates translate into equivalent thematic findings? This study compares eight LLMs to human annotators on a multi-label coding task using 3,200 responses from the UC Berkeley Social Networks Study, comprising over 19,000 coding decisions. Although LLM-human reliability does not match human-human reliability overall, LLMs approach human performance on simpler tasks and can serve as useful additional coders for generating consensus labels. Compared to a gold-standard human consensus, models achieve 82–97% per-category agreement, but macro F1 is lower and response-level similarity is lower still: even the best model reproduces the full human label set for fewer than 60% of responses. Yet high agreement masks thematic divergence. Models systematically over-identify themes, assigning 66% more categories per response, especially for categories requiring greater interpretive judgment. Models also show lower agreement for some demographic groups. These gaps are partly explained by response characteristics such as length, clarity, and atypicality, but the main driver is over-classification itself: models add false positives at a nearly constant rate, so groups whose answers carry fewer themes lose the most precision. At the sample level, models largely preserve the overall thematic narrative: human and model category rankings correlate strongly (pooled Spearman's ρ=0.75), and top-performing models achieve approximately 80% directional agreement on demographic patterns. Concrete behavioral questions, such as reasons for moving or strategies for making friends, show especially strong alignment. Yet systematic over-classification can still shift narratives about how specific groups behave, leading researchers to report patterns that the human gold standard does not support.

articles.title: Improving Efficiency in Egocentric Network Surveys: A Reproducible Qualtrics Template from Design to Analysis
articles.authors: Ruizhe Liu; Mark Girson; Christopher McCarty; Eleonora Rossi
articles.abstract: How can researchers collect social network data in the field and laboratory settings without imposing excessive technical or logistical burdens? This work presents an improved and reproducible approach for collecting ego network data with alter–alter ties using Qualtrics and for preparing the resulting data for network analysis. By leveraging built-in functions of Qualtrics, this approach reduces the effort required to construct and administer large sets of alter attributes and alter–alter tie questions. An offline pilot dataset demonstrates that the instrument functions reliably in low-connectivity environments, and an accompanying data-processing workflow converts Qualtrics exports into network data suitable for analysis in R. Together, this approach lowers barriers to field-, and lab- based social network data collection, mitigates limitations associated with limited programming background and unfamiliar network software, and supports more consistent integration of network measures into broader survey-based research across disciplines.

articles.title: Caregiver-centred networks and the sustainability of later-life care: A conceptual framework
articles.authors: Ruizhe Liu; Brian Khumalo
articles.abstract: Informal caregiving is central to later-life health, yet research has focused primarily on older adults themselves or on caregivers’ individual stress experiences. Less attention has been paid to the structural and relational conditions that shape how caregiving responsibilities are distributed and sustained over time. Building on the Stress Process Model, this paper develops a caregiver-centred framework that integrates four analytically dimensions of network: received support, perceived support, network diversity, and substitute availability. We conceptualize these dimensions as interrelated components of a dynamic feedback system linking caregiver-centred network properties, caregiver burden, and recipient health outcomes. A central contribution is the formalization of substitute availability, defined as the functional capacity of other actors to assume caregiving responsibilities when the primary caregiver is unavailable or overburdened. The framework also identifies contextual conditions, including gender norms, kinship obligations, and demographic change, that shape how caregiving networks are organized. We discuss how this framework can be operationalized through ego-centred and whole-network methods, and outline implications for public health interventions and future longitudinal research.

articles.title: The LINGACON Multilingualism Assessment Standard (L-MAS): Definitions, Thresholds, and a Review of Survey Practice
articles.authors: Areg Hovhannisyan
articles.abstract: How many languages does a person speak? This question—fundamental to understanding human linguistic capacity, global connectivity, and the effectiveness of language education policy—has no standardized measurement protocol. In the course of constructing the first global estimate of Average Language a Person Speaks (ALPS) across 235 countries and territories (a companion study currently in preparation; Hovhannisyan, forthcoming), we discovered that existing data sources use at least six distinct and mutually incompatible methods for assessing multilingualism. These methods produce dramatically different results: For a single country (Zambia), the same survey program (Afrobarometer, n.d.) yielded ALPS estimates of both 2.72 (Round 4) and 5.92 (Round 10), depending on how the question was asked. Meanwhile, entire regions—the Arab states, Latin America, and most of Asia—appear to have no publicly available, standardized multilingualism survey data. We present a taxonomy of current measurement approaches, document their biases and incompatibilities, identify three previously undescribed sources of systematic error (the diaspora residual, the linguistic concealment effect, and the dubbing–subtitling asymmetry), and propose a comprehensive solution: the LINGACON Multilingualism Assessment Standard (L-MAS), a five-level measurement framework scalable from a single survey question (Level 1, zero cost) to a comprehensive national audit with tested proficiency (Level 4) to a longitudinal tracker enabling measurement of multilingualism change over time (Level 5). If Level 1 were adopted by the five major cross-national survey programs, approximately 118 countries—covering over 85% of the world’s population—would have comparable multilingualism data within a single survey cycle. The full L-MAS specification is freely available at l-mas.com.

articles.title: Advancing open research information: exploring the persistence of proprietary bibliographic databases
articles.authors: Tanya Lee; Kathleen Gregory; Alexander Rushforth
articles.abstract:
Purpose – “Research information”, which informs how research is searched,
conducted, monitored, and evaluated, is usually made available in proprietary
databases in ways which often restrict its use. Recently, there has been a movement
towards opening research information through the creation of systems such as
OpenAlex, but their adoption remains inconsistent. In this study, we explore challenges
which university stakeholders face in switching from proprietary to open databases for
research information.

Design/methodology/approach – We conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with
university stakeholders in the Netherlands, a particularly proactive environment in the
Open Research Information movement. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic
analysis and informed by literature in platform capitalism and infrastructure studies.

Findings – The analysis shows that even in seemingly progressive environments,
systemic change remains challenging. Longstanding routines, technical dependencies,
and embedded practices present challenges for universities to disengage from
proprietary databases and their complementary services. Concerns about the viability
and further development of open databases became apparent through the context of
collective action dilemmas perceived by interviewees. Importantly, we find that platform
capitalism, a framework often employed in analyzing proprietary companies, is not
sufficient to explain these hesitancies. 

Originality/Value – Our findings highlight the challenges faced in an under-researched
area of open science: the adoption of open research information. Our study is relevant
to open science advocates and for institutions struggling with similar challenges. Our
analysis makes a conceptual contribution through treating claims about the platform
dominance of proprietary databases as empirical questions and highlighting the
importance of stakeholder agency, contingency and variation.

articles.title: SOBRE LOS REGÍMENES POLÍTICOS EN EL MUNDO Y SU EVOLUCIÓN (1900-2025)
articles.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles.abstract: Este ensayo analiza la evolución histórica de los regímenes políticos mundiales desde 1900 hasta 2025 empleando las bases de datos del proyecto Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem). Revisa los fundamentos teóricos de la democracia y la autocracia, destacando que la tercera ola de autocratización contemporánea no opera mediante golpes de Estado tradicionales, sino a través de una erosión interna y sutil de los contrapesos institucionales. Mediante índices como el de regímenes en el mundo y el de democracia electoral, la investigación examina la distribución bimodal global, las disparidades regionales y la correlación entre elecciones competitivas y garantías liberales, concluyendo que la preservación de la libertad requiere instituciones sólidas y una actuación institucional temprana.

articles.title: Why Play When AI Can Win: The Non-Transferability of Participation and the Visibility of Dignity
articles.authors: Kengo Tomita
articles.abstract: Knowledge work is learning to hand itself over. Drafting, analysis, computation, and even the role of a practice opponent can now be delegated to artificial intelligence, often with better and faster results. This paper asks what does not move in that handover. Drawing on Bernard Suits's analysis of games, I distinguish an achieved state from participation in the activity that produces it and defend an agent-relative non-transferability theorem: another agent may realise the goal state on my behalf, but cannot thereby make it true that I pursued that goal under constitutive constraints I accepted as reasons. AI can deliver the state of affairs; it cannot deliver the fact of participation. The theorem is independent of whether machines can achieve, play, or matter morally. It leaves a human question: under what cultural conditions can people continue activities they know machines can perform better? I use an explicitly extended Kantian contrast between price and dignity to propose that AI, by supplying functionally equivalent outputs at scale, makes newly visible the non-equivalent fact of participation. Japanese professional shogi, which publicly encountered machine superiority and continued, is examined as a completed historical case in which recognition for serious play persisted after technology made its instrumental outputs substitutable. The case illustrates a condition analysis centred on dignity apparatuses: cultural forms that prevent appraisal by comparative performance from exhausting recognition of participants' standing.

articles.title: Impoverishing Growth: An approach from some Developing Countries.
articles.authors: Nerhum Sandambi
articles.abstract: On this approach analysed for example the Impoverishing Growth on majority developing Countries, particularly on some african Countries. This approach helped to understand particularly how for example the high level of impoverishing growth on developing Countries helped to create a weakest economy and weakest social protection, mainly on Country as Angola, where the Social protection naturally not working, this evidence are strongly contributed from high levels of decreasing promoted from respective decrease of the economic growth. articles.title: Different histories, similar discrimination: Field experimental evidence of discrimination against Black parents in the Dutch childcare market
articles.authors: Stefanie L. Sprong; Valentina Di Stasio; Bram Lancee; Eva Zschirnt
articles.abstract: While a vast body of research documents discrimination against ethnoracial minorities, including Black people, existing studies rarely consider how the diverse historical relationships of different Black groups may shape patterns of discrimination. Using data from the first field experiment in the Dutch childcare sector (N = 1,354), we examine discrimination against ascribed Black parents enquiring about childcare spots in the Netherlands. Rather than aggregating all ascribed Black parents into a single category, we compare ascribed Black parents with names associated with former Dutch colonies to those with names associated with Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), expecting the former group to face less discrimination. We find robust evidence that ascribed Black parents face discrimination in access to childcare: compared to ascribed White majority parents, they are significantly less likely to receive a spot offer, and their enquiries are more likely to be ignored altogether. SSA ascribed Black parents are also more likely to experience neglectful treatment in written correspondence. Otherwise, levels of discrimination do not significantly differ between former-colonies and SSA ascribed Black parents, suggesting discrimination against Black parents more generally.

articles.title: Dynamics of Self-Employment Following Motherhood: A Comparison Between Korea and the United States
articles.authors: Wonjeong Jeong
articles.abstract: Parenthood increases the need to adjust paid work, especially for mothers, who continue to shoulder a disproportionate share of carework. This makes it important to understand not only whether mothers remain employed after childbirth, but also how they reorganize work across the life course. This paper examines self-employment as one potential way mothers incorporate flexibility into their post-birth careers. Adopting a life course perspective, I compare new mothers in South Korea and the United States and trace their employment arrangements from first birth to ten years afterward. Using descriptive analysis, sequence analysis, and multinomial logistic regression, I assess whether self-employment emerges as a distinct pathway in mothers’ careers and how its role differs across institutional contexts. The results first show that self-employment is more common in mothers’ careers than cross-sectional estimates would suggest in both countries. However, the way it is incorporated differs substantially. In Korea, self-employment more often follows spells of non-work and is more likely to be full-time, suggesting that it can operate as part of a return to paid work strategy when rse-entry into wage employment is difficult. In the United States, self-employment is more often part-time and embedded within continued attachment to wage employment. Multinomial logistic regression provides only limited support for the idea that self-employment trajectories primarily function as a flexibility strategy, as they are only weakly associated with women’s educational resources and are not clearly associated with second birth. Overall, the findings show that self-employment is part of many mothers’ post-birth careers, but not a general flexibility strategy; its meaning is shaped by institutional context.

articles.title: Influence of Media Modality on Language Learning
articles.authors: Claire Wu
articles.abstract: This paper seeks to examine which form of television media, anime or live action, best aids Japanese language acquisition in English speakers. While this study focuses on the Japanese language, the literature review covers similar studies on the effect of media exposure on English, Korean, and Turkish vocabulary acquisition. In this study, participants were randomly sorted into two groups, an anime viewing group and a live-action viewing group, and were given Japanese vocabulary words to translate both before and after a media exposure phase. Participants in the live-action group gained more vocabulary words on average compared to participants in the anime group. Animated TV allows students to learn at their individual skill level and may better benefit beginner language learners since it often includes more frequent words in the lexicon. On the other hand, the higher language complexity in live-action TV makes it more suited towards intermediate language learners. This study demonstrates that L2 (target language) television, particularly live-acted L2 television, is an effective tool for vocabulary acquisition and reinforcement. In language learning environments, students could benefit from L2 television consumption to aid and accelerate L2 language acquisition.

articles.title: AUKUS: Public Opinions
articles.authors: kerry liu
articles.abstract: This study examines the AUKUS security partnership, established in September 2021, with a focus on public opinion and its relation to national policy in Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Using weekly Google Trends data from September 2021 to July 2025, the research identifies differences in public attention and the key drivers shaping perceptions of AUKUS. Australians emphasise costs and uncertainties; the British prioritise economic opportunities and diplomatic influence; and Americans focus on strategic considerations. China-related factors—particularly the perceived China Threat—play a central role in shaping public sentiment in Australia and the United States, whereas in the United Kingdom, a combination of China influence, employment concerns, and the Global Britain agenda drives attention. The study also considers policy implications, finding a strong alignment between public opinion and government policy across the three countries. While the core AUKUS narrative centres on the UK, the United Kingdom may also play a leading role in setting the policy agenda. These findings demonstrate the utility of time-series digital data for assessing public perceptions and offer a novel approach for understanding the interaction between public sentiment and foreign policy.

articles.title: Diagnosing a Correlation Paradox: How Loose Derivation Chains Conceal Theoretical Anomalies in Criminological Research
articles.authors: Jonathan R. Brauer
articles.abstract: Criminological research programs frequently report statistically significant findings while obscuring systematic patterns that should drive theoretical development. Paul Meehl’s concept of logical derivation chains, or the sequence of logical steps linking theoretical propositions to empirical predictions, provides a diagnostic framework for understanding why empirical tests so often fail to produce cumulative theoretical progress. While recent work has identified criminology’s “precision crisis” abstractly (Brauer & Day, 2025), this paper operationalizes derivation chain analysis as a practical diagnostic method. Using Gottfredson and Hirschi’s (1990) self-control theory as a strategic case study—chosen because its derivation chain is unusually well-documented, making structural problems harder to attribute to researcher oversight—I demonstrate how auxiliary assumptions accumulate to create compound derivation chain failures that render empirical tests uninterpretable. Analysis of the Grasmick et al. (1993) scale reveals a “correlation paradox”: a statistically significant correlation (r = -.31, p < .0001), typically celebrated as strong support, masks theoretical failure for nearly 40% of individual cases. Item-specific analysis across cross-cultural samples from Lviv, Ukraine and Dhaka, Bangladesh reveals substantial heterogeneity and failure of measurement invariance within supposedly unidimensional scales, while cognitive and behavioral measures disagree in classifying individuals in approximately 40% of cases. These systematic anomalies, or high self-control individuals who engage in crime and low self-control individuals who refrain, represent precisely the phenomena that should drive theoretical development, yet correlation-based analytic standards render them invisible. To demonstrate that derivation chain problems extend beyond personality constructs, the framework is also briefly applied to swift-certain-fair deterrence programs (Project HOPE), revealing parallel auxiliary accumulation in policy evaluation research. The paper provides a derivation chain self-assessment checklist and four constraint-aware research practices (individual-level prediction assessment; item-specific analysis; systematic anomaly documentation; auxiliary assumption mapping) as practical tools for building more theoretically progressive criminological science.

articles.title: Officials Hedge, Public Doubts: The Certainty Gap in China's AI-Education Discourse (2020–2026)
articles.authors: Danchen Xu
articles.abstract: Chinese universities have launched a wave of “AI+X” programs that train students in professional domains—architecture, journalism, accounting, teaching—to use generative AI tools, often before any consensus exists that AI-assisted learning improves educational outcomes. Empirical research to date finds no reliable improvement in grades, documents cognitive offloading, and leaves long-term learning effects unmeasured. This paper asks whether that disconnect between institutional acceleration and empirical uncertainty surfaces in discourse: do official and public articulations of AI’s role in education differ in epistemic certainty, and is any such gap innate or emergent? We construct two corpora spanning 2020–2026—official discourse (policy documents and official-media posts, n = 691) and public discourse (Weibo, n = 11,345)—and measure four dimensions of epistemic stance (certainty markers, presupposition, hedging, and tolerance of uncertainty) using a hybrid design that pairs a transparent dictionary with LLM zero-shot coding, cross-validated at a mean Cohen's κ of .926. Three findings stand out. First, before ChatGPT the two corpora were epistemically indistinguishable, replicating Zeng, Chan, and Schäfer’s (2020) “striking similarity”; the gap emerged only after 2023. Second, the gap is not unidirectional: official discourse presupposes AI’s value more (D2 = 82.8% vs. 77.2%; policy documents 90.7%) yet hedges and acknowledges uncertainty significantly more than the public does (D3 and D4 reversed)—a pattern we term institutional hedging. Third, public epistemic stance is bimodal (absolute assertion or absolute doubt), whereas official discourse is layered across premise and expression. Time-series and difference-in-differences analyses locate two shocks—ChatGPT (2023) broke the stance layer (public D2 fell from 82% to 52%), and DeepSeek-R1 (2025) deepened the expression layer (D3 reached its series maximum)—suggesting the public underwent an epistemic learning process, first learning to doubt and then to qualify. We contribute a measurable, multidimensional discourse variable for the certainty gap and a hybrid coding template for large-scale epistemic-stance annotation.

articles.title: Partisan disparities in the production and uptake of science
articles.authors: Alexander C Furnas; Jian Gao; Yian Yin; Dashun Wang
articles.abstract: Scientific institutions are designed to produce and evaluate claims through shared evidentiary and disciplinary standards, yet they are embedded in an increasingly polarized society. This fundamental tension raises the question of whether scientists’ partisan alignment is associated with the production, circulation, and uptake of scientific knowledge. Here we integrate campaign-finance records, faculty rosters, voter-registration data, an original survey of approximately 7,000 active U.S. scientists, bibliometric data, and measures of uptake in policy documents, patents, and news coverage to map the partisan composition of the scientific workforce, the knowledge it produces, and its uptake within and beyond science. We find that U.S. science is politically asymmetric without being ideologically homogeneous: scientists who make political contributions are overwhelmingly Democratic-aligned, and this asymmetry has widened over time, yet the broader workforce includes many Independents and substantial ideological heterogeneity within partisan groups. Among scientists with strong, behaviorally observed partisan alignments, Democratic- and Republican-authored papers are systematically distinguishable in semantic content across all fields, even after conditioning on fine-grained topic and year. Differences in total scientific citation rates are modest and have narrowed over time, whereas citations occur more often within the same partisan author communities than expected under topic- and year-preserving null models. Uptake beyond science also varies by partisan authorship and domain, with the clearest directional selectivity among ideological think tanks. These findings reveal an uneven profile of partisan association across U.S. science, visible in published content and directional attention, but comparatively limited in aggregate scientific recognition. This profile is consistent with a scientific system in which shared evaluative standards coexist with political structure in the production and circulation of knowledge, with implications for science’s capacity to remain a common evidentiary resource in a polarized society.

articles.title: Formal and Informal Institutions Interactively Increase Judicial Independence: Evidence from Israel and Cross-National Data
articles.authors: Andrew O'Donohue
articles.abstract: Comparative research emphasizes that independent judiciaries act as bulwarks against democratic backsliding. Yet we know less about why judicial independence is more resilient in some cases than others. Whereas existing scholarship often contrasts the effects of formal versus informal institutions, this paper emphasizes how their interaction fosters judicial independence. I theorize that one understudied institution—a super-majority requirement for selecting high court judges—increases judicial independence. Moreover, this formal institution better protects judicial independence when complemented by an informal institution—a practice of appointing groups of ideologically distinct judges that I call the Noah’s Ark strategy. I test this institutional theory using cross-national and within-country evidence. Leveraging original data on judicial selection institutions in 139 countries, I find super-majority requirements are significantly associated with increased judicial independence. To show how formal and informal institutions interact, I conduct a case study of the country with the world’s highest super-majority requirement, Israel. Using quantitative data on 16,000 Israeli Supreme Court decisions and qualitative interviews with high-ranking judges and politicians, I show that formal and informal institutions constrained the government’s judicial appointments—but that the government’s undermining of informal institutions weakened judicial independence. These findings illuminate how the interaction of formal and informal institutions fosters judicial independence and democratic resilience.

articles.title: To adopt or not to adopt? Moving beyond a binary conceptualization of farmer’s adoption decisions
articles.authors: Emma Chris Luka Windey; Tina Venema; Agnes van den Pol-van Dasselaar; Hens Runhaar
articles.abstract: Sustainable Farming literature often frames adoption as a binary choice, overlooking decision-making complexity. Drawing on innovation studies, this paper introduces a framework for analyzing adoption decision processes. We examined two types of species-rich grasslands (SRG) as case studies, covering the following decision stages: persuasion, decision, rejection, implementation, confirmation, and discontinuation. We conducted a survey among Dutch dairy farmers (n = 91) and assessed their current decision stage, drivers and barriers to SRG adoption, and farm characteristics. Results indicated that farm characteristics differed across decision stages in nature conservation collective membership for extensive-SRG (E-SRG), but did not differ significantly far any other characteristics for E-SRG, or for any characteristics in the adoption of productive-SRG (P-SRG). For E-SRG, significant differences emerged across stages for several drivers, but not barriers; rejectors stood out most distinctly. For P-SRG, both drivers and barriers varied significantly across stages. Drivers differed most between rejectors and recent implementers, while the confirmation stage was most distinct for barriers. These findings advance theory by showing the value of distinguishing decision stages in the adoption process. Practically, identifying farmer’ current decision stage can guide more efficient policy mixes, enabling targeted interventions that calibrate policy effort to actual needs.

articles.title: Anonymity In Contemporary Political Discourse: Implications of Citizenship And State
articles.authors: Abhay Pratap Singh Tomar
articles.abstract: This paper makes an attempt in bringing anonymity into contemporary political discourse as the issue is getting entangled in political debates more and more which is situated in the debate on anonymity that went on in the house of commons of UK parliament. Hitherto the state has enjoyed the monopoly over space but this paper suggests the rise of the internet and decentralised system databases creates cyberspace which defies the monopoly of state power. Further, it explores the implications for the state, citizenship and anonymity.

articles.title: Who cares? The gendered nature of mobility of care in São Paulo
articles.authors: Joana Barros; Agnes Silva de Araujo
articles.abstract: Quantitative evidence on mobility of care remains scarce and geographically uneven because conventional surveys classify trips by destination and purpose, obscuring caring responsibilities within the evidence used for transport planning. This study expands evidence from the Global South by examining the prevalence, characteristics and gendered distribution of mobility of care in the São Paulo Metropolitan Region. Carrying-passenger trips from the 2023 Origin–Destination Survey are used as a partial proxy for mobility of care and combined with trip-purpose information to distinguish caring activities. Descriptive and negative binomial analyses examine differences by gender, age, race and socioeconomic stratum and interactions between gender and these characteristics, including household car ownership. Carrying passengers accounted for 15.6% of adult trips and displayed distinctive patterns of purpose, mode and trip frequency. Women recorded higher rates than men, particularly for school- and home-related trips, whereas men’s carrying was relatively more work-related. Gender gaps differed in magnitude by race and in both magnitude and direction across the life course. Rather than following a progressive socioeconomic gradient, gender disparities formed a nonlinear U-shape, narrowing to apparent parity in the middle strata but widening asymmetrically at both ends. Car ownership further differentiated gender gaps by socioeconomic stratum and trip purpose. Methodologically, the findings support carrying-passenger data as a useful, although incomplete, means of making care visible in conventional travel surveys. Conceptually, they challenge uniform and gender-neutral accounts of everyday mobility, demonstrating that inequalities in mobility of care emerge through intersections between social positions, caring purposes and household transport resources.

articles.title: Urban veg*ns and rural grillmasters? Local context has a moderate effect on meat consumption
articles.authors: Bram van Vulpen; Willem Rogier Boterman
articles.abstract: This paper deepens the role of what we call ‘local geographies of meat consumption’. The countryside is stereotypically portrayed as a conservative bastion with traditional, meat-centric meals on the table, while urban centres are viewed as progressive hotspots for vegetarians and vegans (veg*ns). Drawing on georeferenced survey data, we demonstrate with a multilevel regression analysis how local community is associated with meat-related diets in the Netherlands. This paper shows the relevance of going beyond the conventional urban-rural constellation, by incorporating a broader and more varied set of local context factors, including political culture, agriculture and food environment. In doing so, we account for individual characteristics such as gender, age, education, and political attitudes. The results show that there are local context effects, albeit to a modest degree. Individual characteristics, most prominently gender, are more strongly associated with veg*n diets. Nevertheless, independent of individual background, people living in highly progressive communities are more likely to follow a flexitarian diet, while those in areas with strong populist radical right support or intensive animal agriculture are more likely to be meat eaters. Our results suggest that the political and agricultural context of local community significantly influences the choice for meat-related diets, rather than urban-rural settings alone.

articles.title: Specification, Heterogeneity and Functional Form in the Determinants of Small-Firm Profitability
articles.authors: Angelo Leogrande; Mauro Di Molfetta; Valeria Nortarnicola; Maria Giovanna Trotta; Antonio Volpe Plantamura
articles.abstract: Studies of small-firm profitability estimate financial structure as the focal regressor and treat cost composition as an unexamined control. This paper reverses the emphasis and places both blocks in one equation, estimated on 91,756 firm-year observations covering 14,913 unlisted Italian firms across three regulatory regimes. Three methods interrogate different assumptions on the same sample: panel estimation across fourteen specifications, unsupervised partitioning selected on eleven validity criteria, and machine-learning regression applied to the same firm-demeaned data. The capitalisation coefficient is not identified. It moves from +0.177 under two-way fixed effects to between −0.12 and −0.28 under five instrument sets, all of which fail because profitability persists at 0.271, so any lagged financial ratio embeds past profit. The labour-share coefficient is stable across estimators, groups and functional forms, and the paper tests whether that stability is arithmetic, since return on assets and the labour share are consecutive lines of one statement. It is not: value added over total assets varies by a factor of 2.8 across the four operating archetypes recovered from the data, while the coefficient varies by 1.07. The accounting identity explains part of the magnitude and none of the stability.

articles.title: Context-Dependent Resource Conversion: Estimands and Decompositions in the Capability-Ecological Dynamic Model
articles.authors: Subir Hait
articles.abstract: Social-science models often summarize the association or effect of a resource with one coefficient or average treatment effect, even when the return to that resource varies across actors, relationships, institutions, and time. This article develops the Capability-Ecological Dynamic Model (CEDM), an estimand-centered middle-range framework for context-dependent resource conversion. Building on capability theory, capital and social-capital theory, stratification, multilevel sociology, heterogeneous-effect methodology, experimental development economics, and transportability, CEDM distinguishes resource possession from access, mobilization, and realized conversion into functionings. It defines an observed conversion surface and the local conversion return, then formalizes conversion modification, ecological shaping, cross-capital complementarity or substitution, conversion instability, context comparison, and dynamic path dependence. Formal results establish aggregate masking; an exact symmetric conversion-structure/composition decomposition; a multilevel decomposition of conversion-return variance; a pseudometric for comparing conversion-return functions; and the logical independence of substantive conversion stability from inferential robustness. Social capital is treated as role-dependent: network structure, accessible resources, mobilized resources, and realized conversion are distinct objects, and social capital may be a focal resource, a modifier of another resource's return, or a contextual property depending on the estimand. Causal interpretation is separated from descriptive conversion and requires a defensible intervention and identification strategy. A reproducible multilevel simulation with 150 contexts and 40 actors per context illustrates the framework: the seeded sample has a pooled mean conversion return of 0.0105, 61.6% of realized conversion-return variance lies between contexts, and 80.3% of that between-context component is associated with ecological support in the specified linear projection. CEDM does not replace established theories or estimators; its proposed contribution is a common estimand-centered language for studying when, where, and through which social conditions resources acquire heterogeneous returns.

articles.title: Cross-Asset Shock Diffusion: A Reproducible Test of Residual Underreaction, Shock Coherence, and Trading Economics
articles.authors: Alina Khaybullina
articles.abstract:
This paper examines whether differences in the speed with which traded assets respond to a common market shock can predict subsequent relative returns. The public framework combines a lagged rolling factor model with Absorption Gap (AG), which measures an asset’s response error, and Shock Coherence (SC), which characterizes the market state on that date.

The study evaluates the signal using executable next-open timing, explicit transaction costs, dependence-aware inference, randomized-signal benchmarks, chronological diagnostics, alternative normalizations, portfolio sensitivity analysis, and machine-learning extensions.

The sample contains 24 ETFs from 4 January 2010 through 28 August 2026, with eight factor proxies excluded from the 16-asset traded cross-section. The paper connects an economic hypothesis about heterogeneous information absorption to an executable quantitative trading framework and provides a reproducible research design for testing cross-sectional predictability, market-state conditioning, and implementation economics.

The contribution is both empirical and methodological: it develops a transparent framework for measuring relative shock absorption, separates cross-sectional signal information from market-state effects, and emphasizes timing integrity, transaction costs, robustness, falsification, and reproducibility in quantitative strategy research.

articles.title: The Down Low Among Latino Men Who Have Sex With Men: A Review and Theoretical Analysis
articles.authors: Keith Robert Head
articles.abstract: Being on the "down low" (DL) describes men who identify as straight and secretly engage in same-sex encounters while maintaining heterosexual public identities. While the DL phenomenon has been discussed primarily in the context of African American men, Latino men in the United States experience similar patterns of sexual concealment shaped by cultural forces not experienced similarly by other groups. Relatively little is still known about how machismo, familismo, and religious values affect the sexual decisions and health outcomes of Latino men who have sex with men (MSM), and most existing research aggregates Latino MSM with other racial and ethnic minorities without examining their experiences separately. This article applies three theoretical frameworks to the DL among Latino men. The concealment-specific model is used to explore how the act of hiding same-sex behavior produces anxiety, depression, and ongoing self-monitoring, particularly within cultural settings where discovery threatens masculine standing and family belonging. Sexual configuration theory is used to examine why Western categories of gay and bisexual do not fit the way many Latino men understand their own sexuality, especially in cultural contexts where sexual role rather than partner gender defines sexual identity. Syndemic theory is used to examine how conditions such as homophobia, HIV stigma, substance use, poverty, and immigration status interact to worsen health outcomes for this population. The findings of this analysis suggest that DL behavior among Latino men is shaped by the interaction of cultural, psychological, and structural conditions and cannot be understood through any single framework alone. Applied in combination, these theories explain DL behavior among Latino men more fully than established Western approaches. This article is intended to support future empirical research and the development of culturally informed interventions for Latino MSM.

articles.title: Cognitive Expectations of Homophily in Village Social Networks
articles.authors: Eric Martin Feltham; Nicholas Christakis
articles.abstract:
Homophily, the tendency for individuals to associate with similar others, has long been
treated as a central principle of social organization. Yet people may overestimate its
importance in reasoning about their social networks. Here, we investigate individuals’
cognitive expectations of homophily and compare these expectations to actual homophily
among 10,072 adults in 82 isolated Honduras villages. We elicited subjects’ beliefs about
whether pairs of people in their village social networks were socially tied. We show that
people deploy cognitive heuristics that substantially overestimate homophily, including
based on wealth, ethnicity, gender, and religion. We also find that people exploit network
structure when predicting ties between others, independent of expectations about
homophily. Understanding cognitive homophily has implications for models of network
formation, interventions targeting social behavior and information diffusion, and the
maintenance of social inequality.

articles.title: The Retreat from Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: Language Change on Large U.S. Foundation Websites, 2019–2025
articles.authors: Chad M. Topaz; Benham Cobb; Frances Lu; Aniya Smith; Nathan Zekarias
articles.abstract: Following the murder of George Floyd in 2020, many U.S. organizations, including large private foundations, publicly foregrounded language related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Beginning in 2023, a series of legal and political developments shifted the institutional environment: the Supreme Court’s ruling in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (2023), state-level anti-DEI legislation, and Executive Order 14151 (2025). Using the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine, we construct a longitudinal corpus of archived web pages from thirteen large U.S. private foundations with established DEI vocabulary and track the frequency of sixty-seven DEI-related terms from 2019 to 2025. Among eight foundations with paired 2023 and 2025 data, six reduced their DEI word intensity; most terms present in the paired corpus declined, with race-related terms contributing the largest share of the drop. The aggregate decline on the full sixty-seven-term index is marginal (exact Wilcoxon p = .074, one-sided); evidence is stronger on the dictionary’s definitional core, the diversity-equity-inclusion triad and its variants (p = .031). The decline concentrates in the 2024–2025 window containing the January 2025 executive orders: eight of nine foundations fell (p = .020), with scattered movement earlier. Qualitative comparison of archived pages illustrates three pathways of retreat: elimination of equity framing, substitution of technical for justice-oriented vocabulary, and reduced prominence through site redesign. These patterns suggest institutional isomorphism operating in reverse—convergent abandonment amid shared political pressure—though our descriptive design cannot identify the mechanism. The findings establish an empirical baseline for tracking organizational communication about equity under political pressure.

articles.title: Digital Influencers, Gambling Perceptions, Behavior and Harm: What Do We Know? A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Anass El Mokhtari
articles.abstract:
Background: Digital influencers (DIs), including celebrities, social media influencers, tipsters, and gambling livestreamers, have become a prominent vehicle for online gambling promotion. This scoping review mapped the empirical evidence on how DI gambling content relates to gambling perceptions, behavior, and harm, with attention to livestreams and to groups at heightened vulnerability.

Methods: Guided by JBI methodology and reported following PRISMA-ScR, four databases and Google Scholar were searched for primary empirical studies published in English or Dutch between January 2016 and June 2026.

Results: Ten studies were included, all published since 2021, five quantitative and five qualitative, with seven conducted in Spain or Australia. DI content was widely perceived to increase the appeal and social acceptability of gambling, and tipster content was further linked to beliefs about skill and control. Evidence on behavior was more limited and largely self-reported. Only three studies applied validated harm instruments on outcomes, and only two addressed livestreams. Reported vulnerability concentrated in adolescents, women, and higher-risk gamblers, but followed largely from the populations sampled.

Conclusions: The evidence is concentrated on perceptions, limited for behavior and thin for gambling harm. All studies were observational, so selection and reverse causation cannot be excluded. Prospective research is needed for further insights, particularly on livestreams.

articles.title: Rethinking Sovereignty through Planetary Thinking: Europe, the Technosphere, and Ecological Redirection
articles.authors: Elodie René; José Halloy; Alexandre Monnin
articles.abstract: This article rethinks European sovereignty under planetary conditions. Rather than treating sovereignty as independence or strategic autonomy, it conceptualizes it as a relational capacity to govern vulnerabilities and interdependencies within the Technosphere. Bringing political theory and international relations into dialogue with Earth system science and ecological redirection, we show how energy, critical materials, digital and scientific infrastructures bind European agency to planetary-scale technical systems. We develop three claims. First, sovereignty must incorporate planetary temporalities and the material reproducibility of technical systems, illustrated through the distinction between living and zombie technologies. Second, the EU’s technological catch-up strategy vis-à-vis the United States and China risks reproducing dependencies and unsustainable trajectories. Third, ecological redirection offers a sovereign practice centered on organized exits, structural sufficiency, care for negative commons, and democratic inquiry into attachments and dependencies. On this basis, multilateralism is recast not as a constraint on sovereignty but as an infrastructure for governing interdependence, negotiating vulnerabilities, preserving scientific continuity, and organizing just technological transitions. The chapter thus proposes a planetary conception of European sovereignty as a dynamic, democratic capacity to compose material viability, political legitimacy, and international cooperation over time.

articles.title: Bioethical guidelines of sexual-attraction change in psychotherapy
articles.authors: Joseph Nicolosi
articles.abstract: This article reexamines ethical and scientific objections to psychotherapeutic interventions that alter clients’ unwanted sexual attractions. While major mental-health organizations label such interventions as controversial, ineffective, and ethically problematic, recent studies demonstrate that some interventions can lead to changes in individuals’ sexual attractions. These interventions significantly differ from the therapies criticized by these organizations. This article examines these criticisms and responds to them, identifies neuroscientific mechanisms that appear to be responsible for sexual attraction changes, and proposes a framework for ethically implementing evidence-based, client-led interventions that influence sexual attraction.

articles.title: El impuesto invisible: La lógica del Neomercantilismo Burocrático en el comercio global.
articles.authors: Federico Estrada
articles.abstract: Este artículo introduce y formaliza el concepto de "Neomercantilismo Burocrático" para explicar la insistencia en la exclusión comercial en economías contemporáneas que mantienen aranceles nominales bajos. El problema central se ubica en la dualidad estatal donde, bajo una fachada de apertura internacional, el Estado implementa una estructura administrativa asfixiante que protege a las empresas dominantes frente a la destrucción creativa. A través de un diseño de investigación mixto, el paper propone de forma preliminar el Índice de Neomercantilismo Burocrático (INB) para cuantificar la brecha entre la apertura nominal y el cierre practico, complementado con un modelo econométrico de panel para evaluar la reasignación deficiente de capital desde la innovación hacia el Lobbying. Los resultados preliminares demuestran que, ante un incremento en las trabas burocráticas, la inversión en I+D de las empresas protegidas disminuye en favor de la protección normativa, validando inicialmente la tesis de la pereza corporativa. Se concluye que el Neomercantilismo Burocrático representa un retroceso cualitativo en la integración global, sugiriendo que el desarrollo interno no requiere únicamente liberalización arancelaria, sino la destrucción integral de la estructura burocrática excesiva que captura el dinamismo competitivo de los mercados.

articles_hidden.title: Compensability in composite lifestyle and well-being indices: a simulation study of power-mean aggregation
articles_hidden.authors: Aamir Saeed Malik; Ahmed H. Hassan; Waqas Rasheed; Shahid Bashir
articles_hidden.abstract: Composite indices of well-being and health almost always combine domain scores using an unweighted arithmetic mean. This choice permits unlimited compensation between domains: a high score in one domain can wholly offset a collapsed score in another. Whether that is appropriate depends on what the index is for, yet the choice is rarely stated as a choice. We examine its consequences for a five-domain lifestyle index, comparing four members of the power-mean family across four data-generating mechanisms in a Monte Carlo study of 100,000 profiles, reported following the ADEMP structure. Three findings follow. First, the arithmetic mean has a uniform gradient: every domain returns the same marginal gain, so the operator supplies no ordering over which domain to improve. Non-compensatory operators identify the weakest domain with probability one. Second, the arithmetic mean permits substantial masking: where one domain has collapsed below 50, between 4.7% and 35.9% of such profiles still score at or above the conventional adequacy threshold of 70, against 0.2% to 9.5% under the harmonic mean. Third, disagreement is concentrated, not general: rankings agree closely for correlated, mostly high scores but diverge sharply for imbalanced profiles. Aggregation therefore encodes a normative judgement about substitutability. Which operator to use follows from purpose: the arithmetic mean to summarise attainment or rank units; an exponent between −0.25 and −0.75 to direct effort at the weakest domain while limiting false alarms; and not the minimum, which flags three quarters of adequate profiles as inadequate once measurement error is admitted.

articles_hidden.title: Simulation-based inference for cultural evolution: a tutorial with baby name data
articles_hidden.authors: Mason Youngblood
articles_hidden.abstract: Cultural evolutionary models are usually easy to simulate but difficult to fit, because most have no tractable likelihood. Simulation-based inference (SBI) addresses this by treating the simulator itself as the likelihood, and now ranges from rejection-based approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) to amortized neural posterior estimation (NPE). Knowing which to use is hard, partly because they are rarely compared on the same model and data. In this tutorial I fit a Wright-Fisher-style model of baby name popularity to uncensored female naming records from South Australia (1944-2017, with inference on 1981-2017), comparing rejection ABC, ABC with random forests, and NPE with BayesFlow on one shared set of 10,000 simulations. The model includes frequency dependence (β), an age-dependent bias (α), and random variation (γ). Recovery varies widely across parameters and methods, from r = 0.96-1.00 for β to r = 0.39-0.97 for γ, and these differences track what each estimator does with the summary statistics it is given and, for γ, how much of the signal those statistics retain. I use the comparison to work through what makes a parameter identifiable, the diagnostics that indicate whether a posterior can be trusted, and common failure modes. All code and data are provided.

articles_hidden.title: Microdosing psychedelics: a case-study exploration of use modalities and the understanding and management of risk
articles_hidden.authors: Dimitrios Liokaftos
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: In recent years, microdosing psychedelics has been a growing phenomenon attracting media, popular and scientific attention. The practice entails the use of sub-hallucinogenic doses of psychedelics substances such as LSD and psilocybin mushrooms. Users report a multiplicity of motivations for and benefits from engaging with microdosing that run across the enhancement/therapy continuum. At the same time, scientific research remains limited and inconclusive as to microdosing’s safety and effectiveness. Methods: The present paper draws on an extended, in-depth interview with a user of psychedelic microdosing to investigate key aspects pertaining to the practice. Results: The discussion focuses on the participant’s engagement with different substances, their understandings of the various risks potentially involved in microdosing, and how they manage these risks. Conclusion: The themes that emerge as significant out of these discussions relate to authenticity, identity and the broader dynamic and antagonisms between the world of psychedelics and dominant culture.

articles_hidden.title: Ação civil pública de perdimento de bens no Brasil: análise crítica da conformidade constitucional
articles_hidden.authors: Eduardo Augusto Velloso Roos Neto
articles_hidden.abstract: A dissertação tem por objetivo analisar a conformidade constitucional da Ação Civil Pública de perdimento de bens relacionados a infrações penais. O trabalho relaciona os antecedentes normativos internacionais e os fundamentos teóricos dos modelos civis de perdimento de bens, avalia o interesse protegido à luz do microssistema processual de tutela coletiva, além de mapear o estágio atual do debate no Brasil. Na sequência, investiga-se o impacto do perdimento civil sobre direitos fundamentais, mormente na presunção de inocência, devido processo legal, direito de propriedade e segurança jurídica. Por fim, o postulado da proporcionalidade é avaliado como critério de controle do modelo, tanto abstratamente, como em relação às possíveis hipóteses permissivas. Foi utilizado o método dedutivo, sendo revisitada a doutrina e precedentes que abordam o tema, além do arcabouço legislativo nacional e internacional pertinente.

articles_hidden.title: Risk-Aware Infrastructure Forecasting for Early Childhood Capacity: A Hybrid Demographic-Housing Model with Algorithmic Governance
articles_hidden.authors: Ang Dong Sheng Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study presents a hybrid demographic-housing forecasting pipeline for preschool infrastructure demand in Singapore, designed for the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA). The model integrates cohort-component population aging with Build-To-Order (BTO) housing delivery signals and Census 2020 subzone-specific child-per-unit ratios, replacing fixed national coefficients that introduce up to 10% estimation error (Wilson et al., 2021). OLS regression models the population-to-child-count relationship (R^2=0.87), while Monte Carlo simulation (n=1,000) transforms deterministic point-estimates into probabilistic planning ranges, establishing a 95th percentile confidence bound recommending a three-center national safety buffer. The pipeline embeds algorithmic governance tripwires — automated buffer-consumption thresholds at 25%, 50%, and 100% — that mandate escalating executive intervention before fiscal floors are breached (NIST, 2023). A Social Return on Investment (SROI) reconciliation maps pedagogical outcomes across five weighted domains to the Heckman Equation, adopting a conservative 1.75x social return estimate (Heckman et al., 2010). Break-even analysis identifies a 3.5-month fiscal inflection point with a 4.62-month margin of safety for construction acceleration investments.
Keywords: Infrastructure Planning, Early Childhood Education, Demographic Forecasting, Algorithmic Governance, Monte Carlo Simulation, Urban Analytics, Singapore Housing

articles_hidden.title: Why Play When AI Can Win: The Non-Transferability of Participation and the Visibility of Dignity
articles_hidden.authors: Kengo Tomita
articles_hidden.abstract: Knowledge work is learning to hand itself over. Drafting, analysis, computation, and even the role of a practice opponent can now be delegated to artificial intelligence, often with better and faster results. This paper asks what does not move in that handover. Drawing on Bernard Suits's analysis of games, I distinguish an achieved state from participation in the activity that produces it and defend an agent-relative non-transferability theorem: another agent may realise the goal state on my behalf, but cannot thereby make it true that I pursued that goal under constitutive constraints I accepted as reasons. AI can deliver the state of affairs; it cannot deliver the fact of participation. The theorem is independent of whether machines can achieve, play, or matter morally. It leaves a human question: under what cultural conditions can people continue activities they know machines can perform better? I use an explicitly extended Kantian contrast between price and dignity to propose that AI, by supplying functionally equivalent outputs at scale, makes newly visible the non-equivalent fact of participation. Japanese professional shogi, which publicly encountered machine superiority and continued, is examined as a completed historical case in which recognition for serious play persisted after technology made its instrumental outputs substitutable. The case illustrates a condition analysis centred on dignity apparatuses: cultural forms that prevent appraisal by comparative performance from exhausting recognition of participants' standing.

articles_hidden.title: Productive Policy Competition and Asymmetric Extremism
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander V. Hirsch
articles_hidden.abstract: Viable policies must be developed by individuals and groups with the expertise and willingness to do so. We develop a model in which competing policy-motivated developers differ in their intrinsic ideological extremism and ability at crafting high quality policies. The unique equilibrium exhibits unequal participation, inefficiently unpredictable and extreme policies and outcomes, wasted effort, and an apparent advantage for extreme policies. While asymmetries between the developers always reduce observable competition, they can nevertheless benefit the decisionmaker. This contrasts starkly with the classic all-pay contest -- where the decisionmaker is always harmed by asymmetries due to the discouragement effect -- and results from the developers' policy motivations. I also introduce and solve a broader class of generalized policy contests that nests both the policy-development model and the all-pay contest, and develop new methods for solving asymmetric contests with spillovers. Broadly, my analysis provides a novel rationale for why extreme actors may dominate policymaking that is rooted in the nature of policy development, and highlights the difficulty in assessing the normative implications of such dominance.

articles_hidden.title: The English Education System in the 16th- and 17th-centuries: Philanthropy and the Study of Science
articles_hidden.authors: Simone Castello
articles_hidden.abstract: This article continues the topic of the reform of education in 17th-century England from the paper ‘Literacy and the education system in 16th- and 17th -century England’, published as preprint on this site in January 2026 (DOI: 10.31235/osf.io/zfs7r_v1). Gresham College and London as the 'third university' in England are the themes.

articles_hidden.title: DE LA MAREA ROSA A SOMOS MÉXICO: EL ESFUERZO PARA CREAR UN PARTIDO
articles_hidden.authors: RICARDO DE LA PEÑA MENA
articles_hidden.abstract: El texto analiza el surgimiento de la organización política Somos (derivada de la Marea Rosa y opositora a la autodenominada Cuarta Transformación). Examina el contexto histórico de las reformas electorales impulsadas por Andrés Manuel López Obrador (Planes A, B y C) y el proceso de obtención de su registro como partido político nacional ante el INE en 2026, enfrentando impugnaciones jurídicas y observaciones sobre su denominación y emblema.

articles_hidden.title: Hours on Equal Footing: Virtual Office Hours and Proximity Advantage in Dual-Modality Universities
articles_hidden.authors: Babu George
articles_hidden.abstract: Office hours are a primary channel for student–faculty interaction, but their modality has received limited attention in fully online courses. The question is most pressing at traditional universities that run online and in-person sections side by side, where a single online roster may contain students living in campus residence halls alongside students who are hours away. This paper argues that the standard, advertised route to instructor access should match the course modality. Virtual hours remove travel and location barriers, ease many scheduling constraints, may reduce intimidation, and appear to sustain participation and in some settings increase it. A standing in-person channel available only to students who live near campus or control their schedules turns proximity and free time into unequal access to help, mentoring, and instructor familiarity. Because students widely believe that being known to an instructor improves how their work is received, such a channel also invites strategic use by those positioned to reach it, and can pressure others to travel in order to keep pace. Drawing on research on online learners, help seeking, social psychology, distance education, and federal and accreditation policy, the paper makes the case for virtual office hours as the equitable and pedagogically coherent default, and sets out the conditions under which optional in-person meetings remain appropriate.

articles_hidden.title: Το ζήτημα της ευημερίας των αναπληρωτών εκπαιδευτικών του δημόσιου τομέα
articles_hidden.authors: Emmanouil Konstantakis
articles_hidden.abstract:
Η παρούσα εργασία εξετάζει το ζήτημα της ευημερίας των αναπληρωτών εκπαιδευτικών στον δημόσιο τομέα, εστιάζοντας στις ιδιαίτερες συνθήκες εργασίας και στις επαγγελματικές και προσωπικές προκλήσεις που συνδέονται με την αναπληρωματική απασχόληση. Παράλληλα, αναδεικνύεται η σημασία της υποστήριξης της ψυχικής, κοινωνικής και επαγγελματικής ευημερίας των εκπαιδευτικών και η ανάγκη ανάπτυξης κατάλληλων υποστηρικτικών παρεμβάσεων.

Η εργασία εντάσσεται στο ευρύτερο πεδίο της συμβουλευτικής, της εκπαίδευσης και της ψυχοκοινωνικής ευημερίας και επιχειρεί να συμβάλει στη συζήτηση για τις συνθήκες που επηρεάζουν την επαγγελματική εμπειρία των αναπληρωτών εκπαιδευτικών στον δημόσιο τομέα.

articles_hidden.title: Contextualising Urban Change: A Novel Classification System for Measuring Built Environment Change Across Great Britain
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Hepburn; Fiona Caryl; Rich Mitchell; Richard Patterson; Laura Macdonald; Alexandros Sfyridis; Daniela Fecht; Jenna Panter
articles_hidden.abstract: Public health policy increasingly recognises the influence of built environments on health outcomes. However, most spatial datasets cannot track context-dependent environmental changes over time, a critical limitation when assessing the health impacts of urban development. This study develops the Built Environment Context and Change Atlas (BECCA), a novel methodology quantifying context-dependent built environment changes across Great Britain (2015-2020). Using the best available national spatial data, we integrated information on buildings, roads, and land cover, applying multivariate clustering to classify both environmental context and changes at 500m resolution. Stakeholders guided the definition of meaningful change categories. BECCA identified that 11% of GB cells underwent change, with substantial variation in development patterns across Functional Urban Areas, ranging from peripheral expansion to infill growth. While developed for Great Britain, this methodological framework is adaptable to other national contexts with similar spatial data availability, offering a template for international environmental change monitoring. By addressing critical gaps in existing environmental change data, BECCA provides a robust foundation for future research linking built environment dynamics to health outcomes, supporting evidence-based urban planning decisions.
